fizik-bilimine-giris.title: Introduction to physics
fizik-bilimine-giris.summary: What does physics study, how does it measure, and where is it useful?

cards.p: Physics studies matter, energy and how they interact. Just as you did a moment ago, it tries to understand nature through observation, experiment and mathematics.
cards.key: Physics is about matter, energy and the interactions between them.

cards.p: A hypothesis is a prediction that can be tested. From results confirmed again and again by experiments, a law tells you what happens, and a theory explains why.

etk.hipotez: Air is what slows the feather down.
etk.deney: Let the air back into the tube and drop both again.
etk.curut: The hypothesis is dropped or changed. The new hypothesis is tested again.
etk.yasa: What happens? In a vacuum every object falls with the same acceleration.
etk.teori: Why does it happen? The theory of gravity explains it.

cards.p: Physics is split into branches by what each one studies. Mechanics deals with force, balance and motion. Thermodynamics deals with heat and temperature. A single event often belongs to several branches.

once.soru: Which branch of physics studies how a refrigerator cools?

secenekler.neden: Thermodynamics deals with heat and temperature. A refrigerator takes heat from the inside and releases it outside.
Optics deals with light. A refrigerator's job is to move heat.
Nuclear physics deals with the atomic nucleus. Nothing changes in the nucleus inside a refrigerator.

cards.p: Physics is woven into other fields. A doctor relies on it when using X-rays and MRI, and an engineer when designing bridges and aircraft. Chemistry and astronomy are built on physics too.

once.soru: An engineer is calculating whether a bridge can carry its load. Which physics topic does she use?

secenekler.neden: The weight acting on the bridge and the supporting forces must balance. That is a mechanics problem.
Refraction belongs to optics and does not affect how strong the bridge is.
Radioactivity is about the nucleus. It has nothing to do with how much a bridge can carry.

cards.p: To measure is to compare a quantity with a known unit. The result always has a number and a unit. "3" is incomplete, while "3 meters" is complete. Everyone uses the same system of units, the SI.

cards.p: The seven base quantities are not derived from any others. They are length (m), mass (kg), time (s), current (A), temperature (K), amount of substance (mol) and luminous intensity (cd).

cards.key: The SI has 7 base quantities: length, mass, time, current, temperature, amount of substance and luminous intensity.

etk.soru: Match each base quantity with its SI unit.

cards.p: You just met speed. Quantities built from the base quantities are called derived quantities. The unit of area is m², of volume m³, and of density (the mass of one unit of volume) kg/m³.

cards.p: We use prefixes for very large and very small numbers. Kilo (k) means 10³, centi (c) 10⁻², milli (m) 10⁻³ and micro (µ) 10⁻⁶.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><text x='80' y='22' font-size='13' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--ink)'>Prefix</text><g font-size='13' fill='var(--ink)'><rect x='12' y='34' width='136' height='30' rx='8' fill='var(--c1)' fill-opacity='0.15'/><text x='22' y='54'>kilo (k)</text><text x='138' y='54' text-anchor='end'>10³</text><rect x='12' y='70' width='136' height='30' rx='8' fill='var(--c3)' fill-opacity='0.15'/><text x='22' y='90'>centi (c)</text><text x='138' y='90' text-anchor='end'>10⁻²</text><rect x='12' y='106' width='136' height='30' rx='8' fill='var(--c4)' fill-opacity='0.18'/><text x='22' y='126'>milli (m)</text><text x='138' y='126' text-anchor='end'>10⁻³</text><rect x='12' y='142' width='136' height='30' rx='8' fill='var(--c5)' fill-opacity='0.15'/><text x='22' y='162'>micro (µ)</text><text x='138' y='162' text-anchor='end'>10⁻⁶</text></g><text x='238' y='22' font-size='13' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--ink)'>Conversion</text><rect x='162' y='34' width='150' height='138' rx='10' fill='var(--panel)'/><g font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)'><text x='172' y='58'>1 km = 10³ m</text><text x='172' y='84'>1 cm² = 10⁻⁴ m²</text><text x='172' y='110'>1 cm³ = 10⁻⁶ m³</text><text x='172' y='136'>1 L = 10⁻³ m³</text><text x='172' y='162' fill='var(--acc)'>1 g/cm³ = 1000 kg/m³</text></g><text x='160' y='192' font-size='11' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--muted)'>prefix is squared for area, cubed for volume</text></svg>
cards.key: For area and volume, square or cube the prefix as well. 1 cm² = 10⁻⁴ m², 1 cm³ = 10⁻⁶ m³ and 1 L = 10⁻³ m³.

once.soru: 1 cm = 10⁻² m. So how many m³ is 1 cm³?

secenekler.neden: All three edges of the cube are 10⁻² m, and 10⁻² × 10⁻² × 10⁻² = 10⁻⁶ m³. For area and volume the prefix is squared or cubed too.
That is only the value of 1 cm. For volume, three edges are multiplied.
10⁻³ m³ is one liter, which is 1000 cm³.

cards.p: Quantities such as mass, time, temperature and energy, where a number and a unit are enough, are called scalars. Force, velocity and displacement (change in position) also need a direction. These are called vector quantities.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><defs><marker id='fgiris-8' viewBox='0 0 10 10' refX='9' refY='5' markerWidth='6' markerHeight='6' orient='auto'><path d='M0 0L10 5L0 10z' fill='var(--acc)'/></marker></defs><rect x='10' y='20' width='140' height='160' rx='10' fill='var(--panel)'/><rect x='170' y='20' width='140' height='160' rx='10' fill='var(--panel)'/><text x='80' y='45' font-size='14' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--ink)'>Scalar</text><text x='240' y='45' font-size='14' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--acc)'>Vector</text><g font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'><text x='80' y='80'>mass: 50 kg</text><text x='80' y='108'>time: 12 s</text><text x='80' y='136'>temperature: 25 °C</text><text x='80' y='164'>energy: 300 J</text></g><rect x='200' y='95' width='34' height='34' rx='4' fill='var(--c4)' fill-opacity='0.4' stroke='var(--ink)'/><line x1='236' y1='112' x2='296' y2='112' stroke='var(--acc)' stroke-width='3' fill='none' marker-end='url(#fgiris-8)'/><text x='264' y='100' font-size='12' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--ink)'>10 N</text><text x='240' y='160' font-size='12' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--muted)'>magnitude + direction</text></svg>
cards.key: A vector carries a magnitude, a unit and a direction.

etk.soru: Is this quantity a scalar or a vector?
ogeler: Energy has no direction. A number and a unit are enough.
Speed is only a magnitude. The one with direction is velocity.
Velocity is given with its direction: 20 m/s east.
Weight is a force, and it points downward.

cards.p: No measurement is perfect. The precision of an instrument depends on its smallest division. To reduce error, you read at eye level, repeat the measurement and take the average.

once.soru: The ruler has only centimeter marks. The pencil tip is between 4 and 5, very close to 4. What do you write down?

secenekler.neden: The ruler's smallest division is 1 cm, and you cannot read anything finer than that. Precision depends on the instrument's smallest division.
This ruler cannot give you hundredths. Those digits would be made up.
No measurement is exact. Every result carries some uncertainty.

cards.p: Physics is a shared effort. Ibn al-Haytham explained vision with light, and Galileo measured motion. Newton studied gravity, Curie radioactivity, and Einstein space and time.

once.soru: An old idea said we see because the eye sends out rays to objects. If so, why can't we see anything in a dark room?

secenekler.neden: To see, light must travel from the object to the eye. Ibn al-Haytham showed this with experiments in the 11th century.
If the eye sent out rays, we would see in the dark too. So the light must come from outside.
When you switch the light on, the objects are still there. Only the light reaching the eye has changed.

cards.p: Physics opens many doors. Research, teaching, engineering, medical physics, meteorology and software are some of them. Organizations such as CERN, NASA and ESA work with physicists. Hospitals, energy companies and software firms hire them too.

cards.key: Someone who studies physics learns to measure, build models and solve problems.

once.soru: What does a meteorologist rely on most when forecasting the weather?

secenekler.neden: A meteorologist measures temperature, pressure and wind, then uses physics models to calculate how the weather will change.
The weather changes every day. Memorizing is not enough; you have to measure and calculate.
A calendar tells you the season. It does not tell you about tomorrow's rain.

cards.p:
• Physics studies matter, energy and interactions through observation, experiment and mathematics.
• A theory explains why something happens, and a law tells you what happens.
• A measurement has a number and a unit. The SI has 7 base quantities, and prefixes are powers of 10.
• A scalar has no direction, while a vector needs one.

quiz.q: Put each quantity in the right group according to its place in the SI.
quiz.e: Mass, time, electric current and temperature are four of the seven base quantities. Speed (m/s), density (kg/m³), force (kg·m/s²) and volume (m³) are derived from base quantities.

quiz.q: Match each event with the branch of physics it belongs to most.
quiz.e: Heat transfer belongs to thermodynamics and the refraction of light to optics. Motion and force are mechanics, and electric current is electromagnetism.

quiz.q: The density of aluminum is 2.7 g/cm³. What is this value in kg/m³?
quiz.e: 1 g = 10⁻³ kg and 1 cm³ = 10⁻⁶ m³. So 2.7 · 10⁻³ kg ÷ 10⁻⁶ m³ = 2700 kg/m³.

quiz.q: What do we call a broad explanation of why something happens, confirmed again and again by experiments?
quiz.e: A theory explains why something happens and is supported by many experiments. A hypothesis is a prediction that has not been tested yet.
y: A hypothesis is a prediction that has not been tested yet. The broad explanation confirmed again and again is called a theory.
Observation means collecting data with your senses or with instruments. It is not a framework that explains why something happens.
A unit is a standard used for measuring. The confirmed framework that explains events is called a theory.

vektorler.title: Vectors
vektorler.summary: How do you draw, add and split quantities that have a direction?

cards.p: A scalar quantity is described by a number and a unit. A vector quantity is described by a number, a unit and a direction. In this topic you will learn to draw vectors, add them and split them into components.

cards.key: Speed is a scalar, and velocity is a vector. "60 km/h" is a speed, while "60 km/h north" is a velocity.

once.soru: Which one also needs a direction to describe it?

secenekler.neden: Velocity also tells you which way something is going ("60 km/h north"). That makes it a vector.
Mass has no direction. It is a scalar.
Temperature has no direction. It is a scalar.

cards.p: We draw a vector as an arrow. The length of the arrow shows the magnitude, and its head shows the direction. The direction is given by the angle θ measured from the +x axis. Two vectors with the same length and direction are equal.

once.soru: You draw two vectors from the same point and complete a parallelogram. Which one is the resultant?

secenekler.yazi: The diagonal from the shared corner
secenekler.neden: The diagonal from the shared tail to the opposite corner is the resultant. It gives the same result as adding head to tail.
The perimeter is a sum of lengths. It is not a vector.
The other diagonal gives the difference of the two vectors.

cards.p: When you multiply a vector by k, its length becomes |k| times as long. If k is positive the direction stays the same, and if k is negative it flips. For example, −A has the same length as A but points the opposite way.

once.soru: A ball moves right at 5 m/s, hits a wall and comes back left at 5 m/s. What is the magnitude of its change in velocity?

secenekler.neden: Δv = v_final − v_initial = (−5) − (+5) = −10. Its magnitude is 10 m/s and it points left. Subtracting means adding the opposite.
The speed stayed the same, but the direction changed. So the velocity vector changed.
The velocity went from 5 to the right to 5 to the left. The difference is 10.

cards.h: Sin, cos and tan in a right triangle
cards.p: In a right triangle, sinθ is the ratio of the opposite side to the hypotenuse, and cosθ is the ratio of the adjacent side to the hypotenuse. tanθ is the ratio of the opposite side to the adjacent side. In a 3-4-5 triangle, the side opposite 37° is 3 and the side opposite 53° is 4.

once.soru: A right triangle has legs of 3 and 4 units. How many units long is its longest side?

secenekler.neden: √(3² + 4²) = √25 = 5. This is the famous 3-4-5 triangle.
You cannot simply add the sides. You need the Pythagorean theorem.

cards.p: You can split a slanted vector into two parts. They are found with V<sub>x</sub> = V·cosθ and V<sub>y</sub> = V·sinθ. If V = 10 and θ = 37°, then V<sub>x</sub> = 8 and V<sub>y</sub> = 6.

cards.key: The components are Vx = V·cosθ and Vy = V·sinθ. Here θ is the angle measured from the +x axis.

cards.p: If you know the components, the Pythagorean theorem is enough: V = √(V<sub>x</sub>² + V<sub>y</sub>²). The direction comes from tanθ = V<sub>y</sub> / V<sub>x</sub>. Check the signs of the components too.

once.soru: Which way does the vector (−2, 3) point?

secenekler.neden: Negative x means left, and positive y means up.
It goes left because x is negative and up because y is positive.
The x component is negative. So the vector goes left, not right.

cards.p: The most reliable way to add vectors is to split them into components and add the x's and the y's separately. For example, if A = (4, 3) and B = (2, −3), then R = (6, 0).

once.soru: A = (4, 3) and B = (2, −3). What is A + B?

secenekler.neden: The x's add up to 4 + 2 = 6, and the y's add up to 3 + (−3) = 0.
That result is A − B. To add, you add the x's and add the y's.
Components are added, not multiplied.

cards.h: When the angle between them is α
cards.p: If the angle between two vectors is α, then R² = A² + B² + 2AB·cosα. For α = 90° this turns into the Pythagorean theorem. If the angle is 0°, R = A + B, and if it is 180°, R = |A − B|.

The forces in the ropes balance the weight, so the total is zero.

cards.p:
• A scalar has only a magnitude. A vector has a magnitude and a direction.
• Vectors are added head to tail or with the parallelogram method. A − B means A + (−B).
• The components are Vx = V·cosθ and Vy = V·sinθ.
• The magnitude is √(Vx² + Vy²).

quiz.q: The vectors A = (3, 5) and B = (1, −2) are given. What is the magnitude of the resultant A + B, in units?
quiz.e: Add the components separately: R = (3 + 1, 5 − 2) = (4, 3). Its magnitude is √(4² + 3²) = √25 = 5.

quiz.q: A 20 N force makes a 37° angle with the +x axis. What is the x component of the force, in N?
quiz.e: The horizontal component is F<sub>x</sub> = F·cos37° = 20 · 0.8 = 16 N. The vertical component is F<sub>y</sub> = 20 · 0.6 = 12 N.

quiz.q: Two equal vectors each have magnitude A. Match the angle between them with the magnitude of the resultant.
quiz.e: R² = A² + A² + 2A²·cosα. At 0° R = 2A, at 60° it is A√3, at 90° it is A√2, and at 120° it is A. At 180° the vectors point in opposite directions and R = 0.

quiz.q: Which of these CANNOT be the resultant of two forces of 3 N and 5 N?
quiz.e: The resultant must lie between |5 − 3| = 2 N and 5 + 3 = 8 N. So 9 N is not possible.
y: 2 N is the smallest resultant, reached when the forces point in opposite directions. So it is possible.
5 N lies between 2 N and 8 N, so it can be reached with a suitable angle.
8 N is the largest resultant, reached when the forces point the same way. So it is possible.

bir-boyutta-hareket.title: Motion in one dimension
bir-boyutta-hareket.summary: How do position, velocity, and acceleration change along a straight line?

olay.h: Which lands first, the hammer or the feather?
olay.p: Apollo 15 astronaut David Scott dropped a hammer and a falcon feather from the same height at the same moment. The Moon has no air, so both hit the ground together.

cards.p: Average speed is distance divided by time. Average velocity is Δx / Δt, and it has a direction. Both are measured in m/s.

cards.h: Velocity and position at constant acceleration
cards.p: At constant acceleration, the velocity grows by the same amount each second, so v = v<sub>0</sub> + a·t. The area under the graph is a rectangle plus a triangle. That gives Δx = v<sub>0</sub>·t + ½·a·t².

cards.h: The equation without time: braking distance
cards.p: When you don't know the time, use v² = v0² + 2·a·Δx. For this car, 0 = 400 − 10·Δx, so it stops in 40 m.

etk.soru: Change the car's speed and its braking acceleration. When the speed doubles, how many times longer is the braking distance?

once.soru: A car moving at 20 m/s brakes and slows by 5 m/s every second. How many seconds does it take to stop?

secenekler.neden: The velocity drops 5 m/s each second, so the car stops in 20 / 5 = 4 s. How many meters does it travel in that time?
The velocity drops 5 m/s each second. How many 5s does it take to get from 20 down to 0?
You don't multiply 20 by 5 here. A velocity of 20 m/s drops by 5 m/s each second.

cards.p: Without air resistance, every object falls with the same acceleration. It is g ≈ 9.8 m/s², and we round it to 10 in calculations. For an object dropped from rest, v = g·t and h = ½·g·t².

cards.p: An object thrown downward also accelerates at g, but its velocity starts at v0. So v = v0 + g·t and h = v0·t + ½·g·t².

cards.key: A stone thrown at 5 m/s reaches 25 m/s in 2 s and travels 30 m.

once.soru: A stone is thrown downward at 5 m/s. What is its velocity after 2 s?

secenekler.neden: The acceleration is still g, so the velocity grows 10 m/s each second. That gives 5 + 10 · 2 = 25 m/s.
That would be the velocity of a stone dropped from rest. This stone already started at 5 m/s.
That is the velocity after 1 s. In 2 s, 10 m/s is added twice.

cards.p: An object thrown upward slows by 10 m/s each second, so v = v<sub>0</sub> − g·t. At the top its velocity is zero, but its acceleration is still g.

once.soru: How does a rolling wheel move?

secenekler.neden: The center of the wheel travels from one place to another, and the wheel also turns around its own axis. Both motions happen at once.
Look at a point on the rim of the wheel. It also goes around the center.
The wheel is not spinning in place. Its center travels from one place to another.

cards.p:
• Displacement is a vector and distance is a scalar. Velocity is Δx/Δt and acceleration is Δv/Δt.
• At constant acceleration, v = v0 + at and Δx = v0t + ½at².
• The slope of a position-time graph gives velocity. The slope of a velocity-time graph gives acceleration, and its area gives Δx.
• In free fall the acceleration is g.

quiz.q: The car goes 35 m forward from the starting point, then 15 m back. Move the car to its final position.
quiz.e: The final position is x = 35 − 15 = 20 m. The displacement is +20 m, and the distance traveled is 35 + 15 = 50 m.

quiz.q: On a car's v–t graph, the velocity rises steadily from 0 to 8 m/s between 0 and 4 s, then stays at 8 m/s between 4 and 6 s. What is the car's displacement in 6 s, in meters?
quiz.e: Displacement is the area under the velocity-time graph. The triangle has an area of ½·4·8 = 16 m and the rectangle 2·8 = 16 m. The total is 32 m.

quiz.q: What do you read from each graph? Match them.
quiz.e: A slope tells you how fast the quantity on the vertical axis changes. On a position-time graph that is velocity, and on a velocity-time graph it is acceleration. An area gives a product. v·t is displacement and a·t is the change in velocity.

quiz.q: With no air resistance, a ball is thrown upward at 30 m/s. What is the maximum height it reaches, in meters? (g = 10 m/s²)
quiz.e: At the top the velocity is zero, so h = v₀² / (2g) = 900 / 20 = 45 m. The climb takes 30 / 10 = 3 s.
y: If you got 90, you forgot the 2 in the denominator. The correct form is h = v₀² / (2g) = 900 / 20.
30 is the number for the initial velocity. The height comes from v₀² / (2g).
If you got 15, you only divided the initial velocity by 2. The height is v₀² / (2g) = 45 m.

bagil-hareket.title: Relative motion
bagil-hareket.summary: Learn who a velocity is measured by. Explore relative velocity on a train, on a river, and in the rain.

cards.h: Are you at rest or moving?
cards.p: You are at rest relative to the room. But Earth carries you around the Sun at about 30 km/s. The same object is at rest for one observer and moving for another.

once.soru: You are sitting in a chair. Are you moving relative to the Sun?

secenekler.neden: Earth carries you around the Sun at about 30 km/s.
You are at rest relative to the room. Relative to the Sun, you move along with Earth.
Earth keeps moving in its orbit at night too.

cards.p: As you just saw on the train, the passenger is at rest relative to a friend but moves at 20 m/s relative to someone on the platform. The observer who measures the motion, together with their axes, is the reference frame.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><text x='10' y='22' font-size='12' fill='var(--c3)' font-weight='bold'>relative to the friend: at rest</text><text x='10' y='42' font-size='12' fill='var(--c1)' font-weight='bold'>relative to the platform: 20 m/s</text><line x1='10' y1='160' x2='310' y2='160' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='2' fill='none'/><rect x='110' y='82' width='190' height='60' rx='8' fill='var(--c1)' fill-opacity='0.15' stroke='var(--c1)' stroke-width='1.5'/><rect x='125' y='92' width='40' height='22' rx='3' fill='var(--panel)' stroke='var(--c1)' stroke-width='1'/><rect x='185' y='92' width='40' height='22' rx='3' fill='var(--panel)' stroke='var(--c1)' stroke-width='1'/><rect x='245' y='92' width='40' height='22' rx='3' fill='var(--panel)' stroke='var(--c1)' stroke-width='1'/><circle cx='145' cy='104' r='6' fill='var(--c3)'/><circle cx='205' cy='104' r='6' fill='var(--c3)'/><circle cx='140' cy='150' r='8' fill='var(--ink)'/><circle cx='270' cy='150' r='8' fill='var(--ink)'/><line x1='160' y1='64' x2='242.8' y2='64' stroke='var(--c1)' stroke-width='2.5' fill='none'/><polygon points='250,64 241,68.5 241,59.5' fill='var(--c1)'/><text x='256' y='68' font-size='12' fill='var(--c1)'>20 m/s</text><circle cx='40' cy='127' r='5' fill='var(--c2)'/><line x1='40' y1='132' x2='40' y2='146' stroke='var(--c2)' stroke-width='2' fill='none'/><line x1='40' y1='146' x2='35' y2='158' stroke='var(--c2)' stroke-width='2' fill='none'/><line x1='40' y1='146' x2='45' y2='158' stroke='var(--c2)' stroke-width='2' fill='none'/><line x1='33' y1='137' x2='47' y2='137' stroke='var(--c2)' stroke-width='2' fill='none'/><text x='10' y='184' font-size='12' fill='var(--c2)'>platform observer</text><text x='205' y='184' font-size='12' fill='var(--c3)' text-anchor='middle'>two passengers</text></svg>
cards.key: The answer to “Is it moving?” always depends on “relative to whom?”

cards.h: Relative velocity: subtract the observer's velocity
cards.p: The velocity an observer measures is called the relative velocity: vrel = vobject − vobserver. If the observer stands on the ground, the relative velocity is the object's velocity relative to the ground.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><text x='160' y='38' font-size='17' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='bold'>v<tspan font-size='11' dy='4'>rel</tspan><tspan dy='-4'> = v</tspan><tspan font-size='11' dy='4'>object</tspan><tspan dy='-4'> − v</tspan><tspan font-size='11' dy='4'>observer</tspan></text><line x1='40' y1='100' x2='152.8' y2='100' stroke='var(--c1)' stroke-width='3' fill='none'/><polygon points='160,100 151,104.5 151,95.5' fill='var(--c1)'/><text x='100' y='90' font-size='12' fill='var(--c1)' text-anchor='middle'>v object</text><line x1='160' y1='100' x2='160' y2='152.8' stroke='var(--c2)' stroke-width='2.5' fill='none' stroke-dasharray='5 4'/><polygon points='160,160 155.5,151 164.5,151' fill='var(--c2)'/><text x='168' y='135' font-size='12' fill='var(--c2)'>−v observer</text><line x1='40' y1='100' x2='153.6' y2='156.8' stroke='var(--c3)' stroke-width='3' fill='none'/><polygon points='160,160 149.9,160 154,152' fill='var(--c3)'/><text x='92' y='156' font-size='12' fill='var(--c3)' text-anchor='end' font-weight='bold'>v rel</text><line x1='280' y1='160' x2='280' y2='107.2' stroke='var(--c2)' stroke-width='2.5' fill='none'/><polygon points='280,100 284.5,109 275.5,109' fill='var(--c2)'/><text x='280' y='88' font-size='12' fill='var(--c2)' text-anchor='middle'>v observer</text><text x='160' y='190' font-size='11' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>reverse the observer's velocity, add it to the object's</text></svg>
cards.key: For “B relative to A,” write vB − vA. This is a vector subtraction. You reverse the observer's velocity and add it.

once.soru: In “the velocity of B relative to A,” which one is the observer?

secenekler.neden: A is the one measuring the velocity. That is why you write vB − vA.
B is the object whose velocity is measured.
The question takes A as the observer, not the ground.

cards.h: Cars moving in the same direction
cards.p: A moves at 90 km/h and B at 60 km/h, in the same direction. The driver of B sees A moving forward at 30 km/h. The driver of A sees B moving backward at 30 km/h.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect x='10' y='28' width='300' height='84' fill='var(--panel)'/><line x1='10' y1='70' x2='310' y2='70' stroke='var(--muted)' stroke-width='1.5' fill='none' stroke-dasharray='5 4'/><rect x='140' y='38' width='50' height='22' rx='5' fill='var(--c1)' fill-opacity='0.25' stroke='var(--c1)' stroke-width='1.5'/><text x='165' y='54' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='bold'>A</text><line x1='196' y1='49' x2='242.8' y2='49' stroke='var(--c1)' stroke-width='2.5' fill='none'/><polygon points='250,49 241,53.5 241,44.5' fill='var(--c1)'/><text x='255' y='53' font-size='12' fill='var(--c1)'>90 km/h</text><rect x='50' y='80' width='50' height='22' rx='5' fill='var(--c2)' fill-opacity='0.25' stroke='var(--c2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><text x='75' y='96' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='bold'>B</text><line x1='106' y1='91' x2='137.8' y2='91' stroke='var(--c2)' stroke-width='2.5' fill='none'/><polygon points='145,91 136,95.5 136,86.5' fill='var(--c2)'/><text x='150' y='95' font-size='12' fill='var(--c2)'>60 km/h</text><text x='20' y='140' font-size='12' fill='var(--c1)'>A relative to B: 90 − 60 = +30 km/h (forward)</text><text x='20' y='162' font-size='12' fill='var(--c2)'>B relative to A: 60 − 90 = −30 km/h (backward)</text><text x='160' y='190' font-size='12' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>same magnitude, opposite direction</text></svg>
cards.key: For cars moving in the same direction, the relative velocity is the difference of the velocities. The sign of the result shows which one is pulling ahead.

cards.p: A moves east at 80 km/h and B moves west at 40 km/h. The velocity of B relative to A is −40 − 80 = −120 km/h, which is 120 km/h toward the west. For cars moving in opposite directions, the speeds add.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect x='10' y='30' width='300' height='60' fill='var(--panel)'/><line x1='10' y1='60' x2='310' y2='60' stroke='var(--muted)' stroke-width='1.5' fill='none' stroke-dasharray='5 4'/><rect x='20' y='36' width='50' height='22' rx='5' fill='var(--c1)' fill-opacity='0.25' stroke='var(--c1)' stroke-width='1.5'/><text x='45' y='52' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='bold'>A</text><line x1='76' y1='47' x2='112.8' y2='47' stroke='var(--c1)' stroke-width='2.5' fill='none'/><polygon points='120,47 111,51.5 111,42.5' fill='var(--c1)'/><text x='80' y='26' font-size='12' fill='var(--c1)'>80 km/h</text><rect x='250' y='64' width='50' height='22' rx='5' fill='var(--c2)' fill-opacity='0.25' stroke='var(--c2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><text x='275' y='80' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='bold'>B</text><line x1='244' y1='75' x2='207.2' y2='75' stroke='var(--c2)' stroke-width='2.5' fill='none'/><polygon points='200,75 209,70.5 209,79.5' fill='var(--c2)'/><text x='240' y='106' font-size='12' fill='var(--c2)' text-anchor='end'>40 km/h</text><line x1='45' y1='114' x2='275' y2='114' stroke='var(--muted)' stroke-width='1' fill='none'/><line x1='45' y1='108' x2='45' y2='120' stroke='var(--muted)' stroke-width='1' fill='none'/><line x1='275' y1='108' x2='275' y2='120' stroke='var(--muted)' stroke-width='1' fill='none'/><text x='160' y='108' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>30 km</text><text x='20' y='144' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)'>B relative to A: −40 − 80 = −120 km/h</text><text x='20' y='166' font-size='12' fill='var(--c3)' font-weight='bold'>they meet in 30 / 120 = 0.25 h = 15 min</text><text x='20' y='188' font-size='11' fill='var(--muted)'>(east taken as +)</text></svg>
cards.key: The time until they meet is the distance between them divided by the relative speed. With a 30 km gap, 30 / 120 = 0.25 h, or 15 minutes.

cards.p: At an intersection, A moves east at 12 m/s and B moves north at 5 m/s. Relative to A, B moves north at 5 m/s and west at 12 m/s. The Pythagorean theorem gives a relative speed of √(5² + 12²) = 13 m/s.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><text x='160' y='26' font-size='13' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='bold'>B relative to A = v<tspan font-size='10' dy='3'>B</tspan><tspan dy='-3'> − v</tspan><tspan font-size='10' dy='3'>A</tspan></text><line x1='30' y1='150' x2='118.8' y2='150' stroke='var(--c1)' stroke-width='3' fill='none'/><polygon points='126,150 117,154.5 117,145.5' fill='var(--c1)'/><text x='78' y='170' font-size='12' fill='var(--c1)' text-anchor='middle'>A: 12 m/s</text><line x1='30' y1='150' x2='30' y2='117.2' stroke='var(--c2)' stroke-width='3' fill='none'/><polygon points='30,110 34.5,119 25.5,119' fill='var(--c2)'/><text x='36' y='100' font-size='12' fill='var(--c2)'>B: 5 m/s</text><line x1='170' y1='40' x2='170' y2='180' stroke='var(--line)' stroke-width='1' fill='none'/><line x1='290' y1='150' x2='290' y2='117.2' stroke='var(--c2)' stroke-width='3' fill='none'/><polygon points='290,110 294.5,119 285.5,119' fill='var(--c2)'/><text x='296' y='134' font-size='12' fill='var(--c2)'>v B</text><line x1='290' y1='110' x2='201.2' y2='110' stroke='var(--c1)' stroke-width='2.5' fill='none' stroke-dasharray='5 4'/><polygon points='194,110 203,105.5 203,114.5' fill='var(--c1)'/><text x='242' y='100' font-size='12' fill='var(--c1)' text-anchor='middle'>−v A</text><line x1='290' y1='150' x2='200.6' y2='112.8' stroke='var(--c3)' stroke-width='3' fill='none'/><polygon points='194,110 204,109.3 200.6,117.6' fill='var(--c3)'/><text x='232' y='150' font-size='12' fill='var(--c3)' font-weight='bold'>13 m/s</text><text x='240' y='188' font-size='12' fill='var(--c3)' text-anchor='middle'>√(5² + 12²) = 13 m/s</text><text x='88' y='188' font-size='12' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>velocities relative to the ground</text></svg>
cards.key: Velocities along different directions cannot be added or subtracted as plain numbers. Draw the vector triangle.

once.soru: At an intersection, A moves east at 12 m/s and B moves north at 5 m/s. What is the magnitude of B's velocity relative to A, in m/s?

secenekler.neden: Perpendicular velocities combine through the Pythagorean theorem: √(5² + 12²) = 13.
Perpendicular velocities are not added as plain numbers.
Perpendicular velocities are not subtracted as plain numbers. Draw the vector triangle.

cards.h: Velocity relative to the ground: add the velocities
cards.p: A train moves at 20 m/s. A passenger walking forward inside it at 2 m/s moves at 22 m/s relative to the ground, and one walking backward moves at 18 m/s. The rule is vobject,ground = vobject,vehicle + vvehicle,ground.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><line x1='70' y1='40' x2='182.8' y2='40' stroke='var(--c1)' stroke-width='3' fill='none'/><polygon points='190,40 181,44.5 181,35.5' fill='var(--c1)'/><text x='196' y='44' font-size='12' fill='var(--c1)'>train: 20 m/s</text><rect x='30' y='58' width='260' height='70' rx='8' fill='var(--c1)' fill-opacity='0.12' stroke='var(--c1)' stroke-width='1.5'/><circle cx='110' cy='89' r='5' fill='var(--c3)'/><line x1='110' y1='94' x2='110' y2='108' stroke='var(--c3)' stroke-width='2' fill='none'/><line x1='110' y1='108' x2='105' y2='120' stroke='var(--c3)' stroke-width='2' fill='none'/><line x1='110' y1='108' x2='115' y2='120' stroke='var(--c3)' stroke-width='2' fill='none'/><line x1='103' y1='99' x2='117' y2='99' stroke='var(--c3)' stroke-width='2' fill='none'/><line x1='124' y1='96' x2='162.8' y2='96' stroke='var(--c3)' stroke-width='2.5' fill='none'/><polygon points='170,96 161,100.5 161,91.5' fill='var(--c3)'/><text x='176' y='100' font-size='12' fill='var(--c3)'>passenger: 2 m/s</text><circle cx='70' cy='136' r='8' fill='var(--ink)'/><circle cx='250' cy='136' r='8' fill='var(--ink)'/><line x1='10' y1='145' x2='310' y2='145' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='2' fill='none'/><text x='20' y='168' font-size='12' fill='var(--c3)' font-weight='bold'>walking forward: 20 + 2 = 22 m/s</text><text x='20' y='190' font-size='12' fill='var(--c2)' font-weight='bold'>walking backward: 20 − 2 = 18 m/s</text></svg>
cards.key: Link the subscripts like a chain. Adding (object, vehicle) to (vehicle, ground) gives (object, ground).

cards.h: The river: relative to the water, relative to the ground
cards.p: The motor gives the boat a velocity relative to the water (vb). The water itself flows with the current (vc). The boat's velocity relative to the ground is the vector sum of the two.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><text x='10' y='26' font-size='12' fill='var(--c4)'>current v<tspan font-size='10' dy='3'>c</tspan></text><line x1='64' y1='22' x2='96.8' y2='22' stroke='var(--c4)' stroke-width='2' fill='none'/><polygon points='104,22 95,26.5 95,17.5' fill='var(--c4)'/><text x='110' y='26' font-size='12' fill='var(--c4)'>3 m/s</text><line x1='10' y1='40' x2='310' y2='40' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='2' fill='none'/><line x1='10' y1='160' x2='310' y2='160' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='2' fill='none'/><rect x='10' y='41' width='300' height='118' fill='var(--c1)' fill-opacity='0.1'/><ellipse cx='40' cy='75' rx='20' ry='8' fill='var(--c5)' fill-opacity='0.3' stroke='var(--c5)' stroke-width='1.5'/><line x1='64' y1='75' x2='116.8' y2='75' stroke='var(--c3)' stroke-width='3' fill='none'/><polygon points='124,75 115,79.5 115,70.5' fill='var(--c3)'/><text x='130' y='79' font-size='12' fill='var(--c3)' font-weight='bold'>downstream: 5 + 3 = 8 m/s</text><ellipse cx='280' cy='125' rx='20' ry='8' fill='var(--c5)' fill-opacity='0.3' stroke='var(--c5)' stroke-width='1.5'/><line x1='256' y1='125' x2='248.2' y2='125' stroke='var(--c2)' stroke-width='3' fill='none'/><polygon points='241,125 250,120.5 250,129.5' fill='var(--c2)'/><text x='234' y='129' font-size='12' fill='var(--c2)' text-anchor='end' font-weight='bold'>upstream: 5 − 3 = 2 m/s</text><text x='160' y='182' font-size='11' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>from the bank you see velocity relative to the ground</text></svg>
cards.key: If vb = 5 m/s and vc = 3 m/s, the boat moves at 8 m/s downstream and 2 m/s upstream. A speed measured in still water is the speed relative to the water.

once.soru: A boat moves at 5 m/s relative to the water, and the current is 3 m/s. When the boat heads downstream, how fast does someone on the bank see it move, in m/s?

secenekler.neden: Velocities in the same direction add: 5 + 3 = 8 m/s.
2 m/s is the speed when heading upstream.
5 m/s is the speed relative to the water. The person on the bank also sees the effect of the current.

cards.h: A round trip in a current
cards.p: The boat moves at 5 m/s relative to the water, and the current is 3 m/s. The boat covers 160 m downstream in 20 s and comes back upstream in 80 s. The total is 100 s. In still water, the same trip would take 64 s.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><text x='10' y='26' font-size='12' fill='var(--muted)'>boat: 5 m/s relative to the water</text><text x='310' y='26' font-size='12' fill='var(--c4)' text-anchor='end'>current: 3 m/s</text><line x1='240' y1='36' x2='293' y2='36' stroke='var(--c4)' stroke-width='2' fill='none'/><polygon points='300,36 290,40.5 290,31.5' fill='var(--c4)'/><line x1='10' y1='46' x2='310' y2='46' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='2'/><line x1='10' y1='146' x2='310' y2='146' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='2'/><rect x='10' y='47' width='300' height='98' fill='var(--c1)' fill-opacity='0.1'/><circle cx='50' cy='96' r='5' fill='var(--ink)'/><circle cx='270' cy='96' r='5' fill='var(--ink)'/><text x='50' y='120' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='bold'>A</text><text x='270' y='120' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='bold'>B</text><line x1='62' y1='80' x2='251' y2='80' stroke='var(--c3)' stroke-width='3' fill='none'/><polygon points='258,80 248,84.5 248,75.5' fill='var(--c3)'/><text x='160' y='72' font-size='12' fill='var(--c3)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='bold'>out: 5 + 3 = 8 m/s → 20 s</text><line x1='258' y1='112' x2='69' y2='112' stroke='var(--c2)' stroke-width='3' fill='none'/><polygon points='62,112 72,107.5 72,116.5' fill='var(--c2)'/><text x='160' y='134' font-size='12' fill='var(--c2)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='bold'>back: 5 − 3 = 2 m/s → 80 s</text><line x1='56' y1='158' x2='264' y2='158' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='1.5' fill='none'/><polygon points='270,158 262,161.5 262,154.5' fill='var(--ink)'/><polygon points='50,158 58,161.5 58,154.5' fill='var(--ink)'/><text x='160' y='174' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>160 m</text><text x='160' y='194' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='bold'>total 100 s, in still water 64 s</text></svg>
cards.key: On the way back, the current costs you more than it gave you on the way out.

once.soru: How does a round trip on a river with a current compare with the same trip in still water?

secenekler.neden: The time you spend going slowly against the current is much longer than the time you spend going fast with it.
The speed gained and the speed lost are equal, but the times are not.
The time lost on the way back is more than the time gained on the way out.

cards.p: The current carries two approaching boats along by the same amount, so it does not change the gap between them. With speeds of 4 and 6 m/s relative to the water and a gap of 200 m, they meet in 20 s.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><text x='160' y='26' font-size='12' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>the current carries both the same way</text><line x1='10' y1='40' x2='310' y2='40' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='2'/><line x1='10' y1='130' x2='310' y2='130' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='2'/><rect x='10' y='41' width='300' height='88' fill='var(--c1)' fill-opacity='0.1'/><polygon points='35,88 60,88 68,95 60,102 35,102' fill='var(--c5)' fill-opacity='0.3' stroke='var(--c5)' stroke-width='1.5'/><polygon points='285,88 260,88 252,95 260,102 285,102' fill='var(--c5)' fill-opacity='0.3' stroke='var(--c5)' stroke-width='1.5'/><line x1='74' y1='95' x2='121' y2='95' stroke='var(--c3)' stroke-width='3' fill='none'/><polygon points='128,95 118,99.5 118,90.5' fill='var(--c3)'/><text x='100' y='80' font-size='12' fill='var(--c3)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='bold'>4 m/s</text><line x1='246' y1='95' x2='185' y2='95' stroke='var(--c2)' stroke-width='3' fill='none'/><polygon points='178,95 188,90.5 188,99.5' fill='var(--c2)'/><text x='212' y='80' font-size='12' fill='var(--c2)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='bold'>6 m/s</text><line x1='130' y1='118' x2='173' y2='118' stroke='var(--c4)' stroke-width='2' fill='none'/><polygon points='180,118 170,122.5 170,113.5' fill='var(--c4)'/><text x='186' y='122' font-size='11' fill='var(--c4)'>current</text><line x1='58' y1='145' x2='262' y2='145' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='1.5' fill='none'/><polygon points='268,145 260,148.5 260,141.5' fill='var(--ink)'/><polygon points='52,145 60,148.5 60,141.5' fill='var(--ink)'/><text x='160' y='162' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>200 m</text><text x='160' y='190' font-size='13' fill='var(--c3)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='bold'>t = 200 / (4 + 6) = 20 s</text></svg>
cards.key: 200 / (4 + 6) = 20 s, whatever the current is. The current only shifts the point where they meet.

once.soru: Two boats on a river head toward each other. If the current gets faster, what happens to the time until they meet?

secenekler.neden: The current carries both boats by the same amount. So the gap between them closes at the same rate.
The current speeds one boat up and slows the other down by the same amount.
The effect of the current cancels out between the two boats.

cards.p: If the boat's bow points straight across, the crossing time is the width of the river divided by v<sub>b</sub>. The current runs parallel to the bank, so it does not change the time. But it carries the boat downstream by x = v<sub>c</sub>·t.

etk.soru: The boat keeps its bow pointed straight across. Change the width and the current. What does the drift depend on?

girdiler.etiket: Boat speed relative to the water

cards.p: To cross in the shortest time, you point the bow straight across, but you drift. To land directly opposite, you angle the bow upstream. Then the perpendicular component gets smaller and the crossing takes longer.

cards.h: Rain and an observer in a car
cards.p: If rain falls at 6 m/s and a car moves at 8 m/s, a drop comes at 6 m/s downward and 8 m/s backward relative to someone in the car. The drop's speed is 10 m/s, and it comes in at a slant from the front. The faster the car, the more slanted the rain.

cards.p: The wind that hits your face on a bike is the velocity of the air relative to you. On a ship, the smoke and the flag also stream along the wind's velocity relative to the ship.

once.soru: On a day with no wind, you ride a bike north. Where do you feel the wind coming from?

secenekler.neden: Relative to you, the air flows south, so it hits your face from the front.
Relative to you, the air moves the opposite way, so it comes from the front.
The air is still, but you are moving. So the relative velocity is not zero.

cards.p: Watch out for four traps. Don't write v<sub>A</sub> − v<sub>B</sub> for “B relative to A.” Don't subtract speeds in opposite directions. Don't add perpendicular velocities as plain numbers. Don't include the current in the crossing time.

cards.key: In relative velocity, the sign shows the direction. State the direction when you write the result.

once.soru: A moves east at 30 km/h and B moves west at 50 km/h. What is the velocity of B relative to A?

secenekler.neden: vB − vA = −50 − 30 = −80. So the velocity is 80 km/h toward the west.
Speeds in opposite directions add. They are not subtracted.
The magnitude is right, but A sees B moving west.

cards.p:
• Velocity is measured relative to an observer, so the reference must be stated.
• Relative velocity is the object's velocity minus the observer's velocity, as vectors.
• Velocity relative to the ground is the velocity relative to the vehicle plus the vehicle's velocity.
• Crossing time is the width divided by the perpendicular velocity, and the current causes drift.
• From a vehicle, rain appears with its relative velocity.

quiz.q: On a river 120 m wide, the current is 2 m/s. A boat with a speed of 6 m/s relative to the water crosses with its bow pointed straight across. How many meters does the boat drift downstream?
quiz.e: The crossing time is t = 120 / 6 = 20 s, and the current does not change it. The drift is x = 2 · 20 = 40 m.

quiz.q: Two cars move at 8 m/s and 6 m/s. Match each case with the magnitude of their velocity relative to each other.
quiz.e: In the same direction, the relative speed is 8 − 6 = 2 m/s. In opposite directions, it is 8 + 6 = 14 m/s. For perpendicular velocities, the Pythagorean theorem gives √(8² + 6²) = 10 m/s.

quiz.q: A train moves at 20 m/s relative to the ground. Put these people in order of speed relative to the ground, from slowest to fastest.
ogeler: A person standing on the platform
A passenger walking backward on the train at 2 m/s
A passenger sitting on the train
A passenger walking forward on the train at 2 m/s
quiz.e: Velocity relative to the ground is the velocity relative to the train plus the train's velocity. The platform is at 0, the passenger walking backward at 20 − 2 = 18, the seated passenger at 20, and the passenger walking forward at 20 + 2 = 22 m/s.

quiz.q: With no wind, raindrops fall straight down at 10 m/s. How does a passenger in a car moving east at 10 m/s see the drops?
o: At 45° from the vertical, toward the east, at 20 m/s
At 45° from the vertical, toward the west, at 20 m/s
At 45° from the vertical, toward the west, at about 14.1 m/s
quiz.e: The rain's velocity relative to the passenger is v<sub>rain</sub> − v<sub>car</sub>: 10 m/s downward and 10 m/s toward the west. Its magnitude is √(10² + 10²) ≈ 14.1 m/s. The rain makes a 45° angle with the vertical and slants west, toward the back of the car.
y: The passenger is moving too, so relative to them the drops also have a horizontal velocity component.
Relative velocity comes from subtracting the passenger's velocity. The drops slant toward the back, which is west.
Perpendicular components are combined with the Pythagorean theorem, not added as plain numbers. The result is √(10²+10²) ≈ 14.1 m/s.

newton-yasalari.title: Newton's laws of motion
newton-yasalari.summary: How does a force change motion? The three laws and the fundamental forces.

cards.p: A force is a push or a pull. It has a direction, so it is a vector. The vector sum of all the forces is called the net force. The net force decides how the object moves.

cards.key: Net force = the vector sum of all the forces acting on the object

cards.h: The four fundamental forces of nature
cards.p: Every force comes from four interactions. They are gravity, the electromagnetic interaction (all contact forces), the strong nuclear interaction, and the weak nuclear interaction. Gravity is the weakest.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><rect x='10' y='14' width='300' height='38' rx='8' fill='var(--c2)' fill-opacity='0.15' stroke='var(--c2)'/><text x='20' y='38' font-size='13' font-weight='bold' fill='var(--ink)'>Strong nuclear</text><text x='140' y='38' font-size='11' fill='var(--muted)'>holds the nucleus</text><text x='302' y='38' font-size='10' text-anchor='end' fill='var(--c2)' font-weight='bold'>strongest</text><rect x='10' y='60' width='300' height='38' rx='8' fill='var(--c1)' fill-opacity='0.15' stroke='var(--c1)'/><text x='20' y='84' font-size='13' font-weight='bold' fill='var(--ink)'>Electromagnetic</text><text x='140' y='84' font-size='11' fill='var(--muted)'>friction, normal, tension</text><rect x='10' y='106' width='300' height='38' rx='8' fill='var(--c5)' fill-opacity='0.15' stroke='var(--c5)'/><text x='20' y='130' font-size='13' font-weight='bold' fill='var(--ink)'>Weak nuclear</text><text x='140' y='130' font-size='11' fill='var(--muted)'>radioactive decay</text><rect x='10' y='152' width='300' height='38' rx='8' fill='var(--c3)' fill-opacity='0.15' stroke='var(--c3)'/><text x='20' y='176' font-size='13' font-weight='bold' fill='var(--ink)'>Gravity</text><text x='140' y='176' font-size='11' fill='var(--muted)'>weight, planets</text><text x='302' y='176' font-size='10' text-anchor='end' fill='var(--c3)' font-weight='bold'>weakest</text></svg>
cards.key: The strongest is the strong nuclear force, which holds the nucleus together. Gravity is the weakest, but it always attracts and its range has no limit.

once.soru: Which interaction do contact forces like friction and the normal force come from?

secenekler.neden: The electrons in the atoms of two touching surfaces repel each other. That is why all contact forces are electromagnetic.
Gravity produces weight, and it does not need contact.
The strong nuclear force only acts inside the nucleus.

cards.p: If the net force is zero, an object at rest stays at rest and a moving object keeps going in a straight line at constant velocity. This is called inertia. It is why you lurch forward when a car brakes.

cards.key: If the net force is zero, the velocity does not change. Being at rest is also constant velocity (v = 0).

cards.p: A net force accelerates an object, and a = Fnet / m. The acceleration points the same way as the net force. With the same push, an empty shopping cart speeds up more easily than a full one.

cards.key: 1 N = 1 kg·m/s². A force of 1 N gives a 1 kg object an acceleration of 1 m/s². A 100 g apple weighs about 1 N.

etk.soru: Change the net force and the mass: a = F<sub>net</sub> / m.

cards.p: As you just saw, if A pushes on B, then B pushes on A with an equal and opposite force. The two forces act on different objects, so they do not cancel.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><circle cx='110' cy='58' r='10' fill='var(--c1)' fill-opacity='0.3'/><circle cx='210' cy='58' r='10' fill='var(--c3)' fill-opacity='0.3'/><rect x='90' y='70' width='40' height='80' fill='var(--c1)' fill-opacity='0.25' rx='8'/><rect x='190' y='70' width='40' height='80' fill='var(--c3)' fill-opacity='0.25' rx='8'/><line x1='130' y1='100' x2='190' y2='100' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='2' fill='none'/><line x1='90' y1='110' x2='47' y2='110' stroke='var(--acc)' stroke-width='3' fill='none'/><polygon points='40,110 50,105.5 50,114.5' fill='var(--acc)'/><line x1='230' y1='110' x2='273' y2='110' stroke='var(--acc)' stroke-width='3' fill='none'/><polygon points='280,110 270,114.5 270,105.5' fill='var(--acc)'/><text x='65' y='100' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='bold'>B→A</text><text x='255' y='100' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='bold'>A→B</text><text x='110' y='170' font-size='13' fill='var(--c1)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='bold'>A</text><text x='210' y='170' font-size='13' fill='var(--c3)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='bold'>B</text><text x='160' y='192' font-size='12' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>same magnitude, opposite direction, different objects</text></svg>
cards.key: Action and reaction forces are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction. They also act on different objects.

cards.p: Mass (kg) is the amount of matter, and it is the same everywhere. Weight (N) is the force of gravity: W = m·g. In this topic we take g = 10 m/s².
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><text x='90' y='16' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='bold'>Earth (g ≈ 10)</text><text x='230' y='16' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='bold'>Mars (g ≈ 3.7)</text><text x='90' y='33' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>m = 50 kg</text><text x='230' y='33' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>m = 50 kg</text><circle cx='90' cy='50' r='10' fill='var(--c1)' fill-opacity='0.35' stroke='var(--c1)' stroke-width='1.5'/><circle cx='230' cy='50' r='10' fill='var(--c1)' fill-opacity='0.35' stroke='var(--c1)' stroke-width='1.5'/><line x1='90' y1='62' x2='90' y2='175' stroke='var(--c2)' stroke-width='3' fill='none'/><polygon points='90,182 85.5,172 94.5,172' fill='var(--c2)'/><line x1='230' y1='62' x2='230' y2='97' stroke='var(--c2)' stroke-width='3' fill='none'/><polygon points='230,104 225.5,94 234.5,94' fill='var(--c2)'/><text x='100' y='130' font-size='13' fill='var(--c2)' font-weight='bold'>W = 500 N</text><text x='240' y='92' font-size='13' fill='var(--c2)' font-weight='bold'>W ≈ 185 N</text><text x='230' y='140' font-size='12' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>same mass,</text><text x='230' y='158' font-size='12' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>different weight</text></svg>
cards.key: Weight is W = m·g. A 50 kg person weighs 500 N on Earth and about 185 N on Mars (g ≈ 3.7).

cards.p: A surface pushes on an object resting on it with a force perpendicular to the surface. This is the normal force (N). On level ground with no other vertical force, N = W.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect x='40' y='120' width='240' height='10' fill='var(--panel)' stroke='var(--muted)' stroke-width='1.5'/><line x1='60' y1='130' x2='60' y2='190' stroke='var(--muted)' stroke-width='3' fill='none'/><line x1='260' y1='130' x2='260' y2='190' stroke='var(--muted)' stroke-width='3' fill='none'/><rect x='130' y='95' width='60' height='25' fill='var(--c5)' fill-opacity='0.3' stroke='var(--c5)' stroke-width='1.5'/><line x1='160' y1='107' x2='160' y2='54' stroke='var(--c3)' stroke-width='3' fill='none'/><polygon points='160,47 164.5,57 155.5,57' fill='var(--c3)'/><line x1='160' y1='107' x2='160' y2='160' stroke='var(--c2)' stroke-width='3' fill='none'/><polygon points='160,167 155.5,157 164.5,157' fill='var(--c2)'/><text x='168' y='57' font-size='13' fill='var(--c3)' font-weight='bold'>N</text><text x='168' y='165' font-size='13' fill='var(--c2)' font-weight='bold'>W = m·g</text><text x='230' y='75' font-size='13' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='bold'>N = W</text><text x='230' y='93' font-size='12' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>(level table)</text></svg>
cards.key: N and W are not an action-reaction pair, because both act on the book.

once.soru: A 2 kg book rests on a table. How many newtons of upward force does the table put on it? (g = 10)

secenekler.neden: The book is not falling. The table's upward push balances the weight (2 · 10 = 20 N).
If the table did not push, the book would fall.
2 is the book's mass (kg). Its weight is m·g = 20 N.

cards.p: Friction acts opposite to the motion. For a sliding object, fk = μk·N, and μk depends on the kind of surfaces. With a mass of 10 kg and μk = 0.3, fk = 30 N.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><line x1='20' y1='135' x2='300' y2='135' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='1.5' fill='none'/><rect x='130' y='95' width='60' height='40' fill='var(--c4)' fill-opacity='0.3' stroke='var(--c4)' stroke-width='1.5'/><line x1='160' y1='95' x2='160' y2='33.4' stroke='var(--c3)' stroke-width='2.5' fill='none'/><polygon points='160,26.4 164.5,36.4 155.5,36.4' fill='var(--c3)'/><line x1='160' y1='115' x2='160' y2='176.6' stroke='var(--c2)' stroke-width='2.5' fill='none'/><polygon points='160,183.6 155.5,173.6 164.5,173.6' fill='var(--c2)'/><line x1='190' y1='115' x2='218' y2='115' stroke='var(--c1)' stroke-width='2.5' fill='none'/><polygon points='225,115 215,119.5 215,110.5' fill='var(--c1)'/><line x1='130' y1='131' x2='116.4' y2='131' stroke='var(--acc)' stroke-width='2.5' fill='none'/><polygon points='109.4,131 119.4,126.5 119.4,135.5' fill='var(--acc)'/><text x='168' y='40' font-size='12' fill='var(--c3)' font-weight='bold'>N = 100 N</text><text x='168' y='182' font-size='12' fill='var(--c2)' font-weight='bold'>W = 100 N</text><text x='230' y='119' font-size='12' fill='var(--c1)' font-weight='bold'>F = 50 N</text><text x='105' y='124' font-size='12' fill='var(--acc)' text-anchor='end' font-weight='bold'>fk = 30 N</text><text x='230' y='60' font-size='12' fill='var(--muted)'>motion</text><line x1='230' y1='70' x2='284.4' y2='70' stroke='var(--muted)' stroke-width='1.5' fill='none'/><polygon points='290,70 282,73.6 282,66.4' fill='var(--muted)'/><text x='232' y='160' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)'>μk = 0.3</text></svg>
cards.key: Friction does not depend on the contact area. It only depends on the kind of surfaces (μ) and on N.

once.soru: Which way does friction act on a sliding box?

secenekler.neden: Friction resists sliding, so it acts opposite to the motion.
If it did, it would speed the box up.
Friction is parallel to the surface. The upward push is the normal force.

cards.p: When you push a cabinet that is at rest, static friction grows to match your push, up to a maximum of μs·N. Once your push goes above that, the cabinet slides. Usually μk < μs.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><path d='M40 170 H300 M40 170 V30' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M40 170 L160 60 L172 85 H290' fill='none' stroke='var(--c2)' stroke-width='2.5'/><path d='M160 60 V170' stroke='var(--line)' stroke-dasharray='3 3'/><text x='100' y='150' font-size='11' fill='var(--c2)' text-anchor='middle'>static: fs = F</text><text x='165' y='52' font-size='11' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='start' font-weight='700'>fs,max = μs·N</text><text x='230' y='78' font-size='11' fill='var(--c2)' text-anchor='middle'>kinetic: fk = μk·N</text><text x='100' y='186' font-size='11' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>object at rest</text><text x='230' y='186' font-size='11' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>object slides</text><text x='32' y='36' font-size='12' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='end'>f</text><text x='300' y='160' font-size='10' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='end'>applied F</text></svg>
cards.key: For an object at rest, 0 ≤ fs ≤ μs·N. For a sliding object, fk = μk·N. That is why starting the motion is harder than keeping it going.

cards.p: Draw the object as a dot and add only the forces acting on it as arrows. Then write Fnet = m·a for each axis.

cards.key: Draw the forces acting on the object, not the forces it exerts. On an incline, N = W·cosθ, which is smaller than W.

etk.soru: The free-body diagram of a 10 kg box at rest on an incline. Explore the arrows.

noktalar.acik: It rests on a 30° incline. In the diagram it is drawn as a dot, and the forces start from that dot.
The weight is W = m·g = 10·10 = 100 N, and it points straight down.
The normal force is perpendicular to the surface, and N = W·cos30° ≈ 87 N. On an incline, N is smaller than W.
Friction keeps the box from sliding, so it points up the slope. Its magnitude is f = W·sin30° = 50 N.

once.soru: Which of these is not drawn on the free-body diagram of a book on a table?

secenekler.yazi: The book's push on the table
secenekler.neden: That force acts on the table. The diagram only shows forces that act on the book.
Weight acts on the book, so it is drawn.

secenekler.yazi: The table's push on the book
secenekler.neden: The normal force acts on the book, so it is drawn.

cards.p: On an incline, the parallel component of the weight, W·sinθ, pulls the object down the slope. Without friction, a = g·sinθ, and the acceleration does not depend on mass. With friction, a = g·sinθ − μk·g·cosθ.

once.soru: A truck and a marble are released on a frictionless 30° incline. Which one has the larger acceleration?

secenekler.neden: a = g·sinθ. Mass appears in both the force and the inertia, so it cancels.
The force pulling the truck is large, but so is its mass. So the acceleration is the same.
Being light does not increase the acceleration, because a = g·sinθ.

cards.p: A taut rope pulls the object tied to it along the rope with a tension force (T). Objects connected by a rope move with the same acceleration. First find the acceleration from a = Fnet / mtotal, then find T.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><text x='160' y='30' font-size='12' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>frictionless floor</text><line x1='20' y1='160' x2='300' y2='160' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='1.5' fill='none'/><rect x='40' y='120' width='50' height='40' fill='var(--c5)' fill-opacity='0.3' stroke='var(--c5)' stroke-width='1.5'/><rect x='150' y='112' width='64' height='48' fill='var(--c4)' fill-opacity='0.3' stroke='var(--c4)' stroke-width='1.5'/><text x='65' y='145' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='bold'>2 kg</text><text x='182' y='141' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='bold'>3 kg</text><line x1='90' y1='140' x2='150' y2='140' stroke='var(--muted)' stroke-width='2' fill='none'/><line x1='92' y1='124' x2='109' y2='124' stroke='var(--c2)' stroke-width='2.5' fill='none'/><polygon points='116,124 106,128.5 106,119.5' fill='var(--c2)'/><line x1='148' y1='124' x2='131' y2='124' stroke='var(--c2)' stroke-width='2.5' fill='none'/><polygon points='124,124 134,119.5 134,128.5' fill='var(--c2)'/><text x='102' y='114' font-size='13' fill='var(--c2)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='bold'>T</text><text x='138' y='114' font-size='13' fill='var(--c2)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='bold'>T</text><line x1='214' y1='136' x2='283' y2='136' stroke='var(--c3)' stroke-width='3' fill='none'/><polygon points='290,136 280,140.5 280,131.5' fill='var(--c3)'/><text x='252' y='126' font-size='12' fill='var(--c3)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='bold'>F = 20 N</text><text x='160' y='180' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>a = 20 / (2 + 3) = 4 m/s²</text><text x='160' y='196' font-size='12' fill='var(--c2)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='bold'>T = 2 · 4 = 8 N</text></svg>
cards.key: The rope pulls on the two objects with equal and opposite T. T is an internal force, so it does not change the acceleration of the system.

once.soru: Two boxes of 2 kg and 3 kg are tied together with a rope. They are pulled with 10 N on a frictionless floor. What is the acceleration, in m/s²?

secenekler.neden: Think of the two boxes as one object. a = 10 / (2 + 3) = 2 m/s².
The 10 N accelerates the whole 5 kg, not just the 2 kg.
10 / 3 only accounts for one box. But the two boxes move together.

cards.p: Two objects of 3 kg and 2 kg hang from a pulley. The net force is the difference of the weights, so a = (m₁ − m₂)·g / (m₁ + m₂). The heavier object moves down.

once.soru: 3 kg and 2 kg hang on the two sides of a pulley. What net force accelerates the system, in N? (g = 10)

secenekler.neden: The weights are 30 N and 20 N. They pull in opposite directions, so the net force is their difference, 10 N.
The weights pull in opposite directions on the two sides of the rope. So they do not add.
30 N is only the weight of the heavier object. The other object holds it back.

cards.p: A scale reads the normal force. When the elevator accelerates upward, N = m·(g + a). When it accelerates downward, N = m·(g − a). In free fall, N = 0.

once.soru: A 60 kg person stands on a scale in an elevator accelerating upward at 2 m/s². What does the scale read, in N? (g = 10)

secenekler.neden: The floor has to both support the person and accelerate them. So N = 60·(10 + 2) = 720 N.
600 N is the reading in an elevator at rest or moving at constant velocity.
That is the reading in an elevator accelerating downward: 60·(10 − 2).

cards.p: Air resistance grows with speed. When it equals the weight, the net force is zero and the object falls at a constant terminal velocity. A parachute increases the cross-sectional area and lowers the terminal velocity.

once.soru: After falling for a while, a skydiver's speed stops increasing. What is the net force?

secenekler.neden: If the velocity is constant, the acceleration is zero. So air resistance has become equal to the weight.
If the net force equaled the weight, the skydiver would keep speeding up.
With an upward net force, the skydiver would slow down.

cards.p:
• First law: if the net force is zero, the velocity does not change.
• Second law: Fnet = m·a.
• Third law: action and reaction are equal, opposite, and act on different objects.
• Weight is W = m·g.
• For friction, fs ≤ μs·N and fk = μk·N.

quiz.q: Masses of 4 kg and 1 kg hang on the two sides of an ideal pulley. What is the acceleration of the system, in m/s²? (g = 10 m/s²)
quiz.e: a = (m₁ − m₂)·g / (m₁ + m₂) = (4 − 1)·10 / 5 = 6 m/s². The heavier 4 kg mass moves down.

quiz.q: A 10 kg box is pulled with a horizontal force of 50 N across a floor where the coefficient of kinetic friction is μk = 0.2. If g = 10 m/s², what is the box's acceleration, in m/s²?
quiz.e: N = m·g = 100 N and f<sub>k</sub> = 0.2·100 = 20 N. The net force is 50 − 20 = 30 N, and the acceleration is 30 / 10 = 3 m/s².

quiz.q: A 60 kg person stands on a scale in an elevator. Put the scale readings in order from smallest to largest. (g = 10 m/s²)
ogeler: The elevator is in free fall
The elevator accelerates downward at 2 m/s²
The elevator moves at constant velocity
The elevator accelerates upward at 2 m/s²
quiz.e: A scale reads the normal force. In free fall N = 0, and accelerating downward N = 60·(10 − 2) = 480 N. At constant velocity it is 600 N, and accelerating upward it is 60·(10 + 2) = 720 N.

quiz.q: When a horse pulls a cart, the cart pulls back on the horse with the same magnitude. Why don't these two forces cancel?
o: The horse's force is slightly larger
The cart is light, so there is no reaction
quiz.e: Action and reaction forces act on different objects. What moves the horse forward is the friction force the ground puts on its hooves.
y: Action and reaction forces are always exactly equal in magnitude. There is no difference between them.
Action and reaction appear at the same moment. There is no delay between them.
However small the mass is, the reaction force is always there and equals the action.

iki-boyutta-hareket.title: Motion in two dimensions and projectiles
iki-boyutta-hareket.summary: Why do thrown objects follow a parabola, and how far do they go?

cards.h: The curved path of a thrown object
cards.p: A thrown ball follows a curved path called a parabola. The way to solve it is to split the motion into two: horizontal and vertical. In this topic g = 9.8 m/s² and there is no air resistance.

once.soru: What does the path of a ball thrown horizontally look like?

secenekler.neden: The ball keeps moving horizontally while it falls faster and faster vertically. So its path is a parabola.
The vertical velocity keeps growing, so the path bends instead of staying straight.
Gravity acts from the very first moment. So no part of the path is straight.

cards.p: As you just saw, a dropped ball and a ball thrown horizontally land at the same moment. Only gravity sets the vertical motion. The horizontal velocity does not change the fall.

cards.key: The object moves at constant velocity horizontally and is in free fall vertically. Solve the two motions separately.

cards.p: An object thrown horizontally moves at constant velocity in the horizontal direction, so x = v<sub>0</sub>·t. Vertically it is in free fall, so h = ½·g·t².
