quiz.q: A 2 kg box is released from rest at the top of a 5 m high ramp and reaches the bottom at 8 m/s. How many joules did friction turn into heat? (g = 10 m/s²)
quiz.e: The initial energy is m·g·h = 2·10·5 = 100 J, and the final energy is ½·2·8² = 64 J. Friction turned 100 − 64 = 36 J into heat.

quiz.q: You apply the force. Are you doing work in the physics sense?
ogeler: Lifting a book onto a shelf
Holding a weight in the air
quiz.e: For work to be done, there must be a displacement along the direction of the force. The book, the box, and the ball move in the direction of the force. The wall and the weight held in the air do not move. Even if you get tired, W = 0 in these cases.

quiz.q: A net force of 20 N acts on a 4 kg object at rest over 10 m. What is the object's final speed, in m/s?
quiz.e: The net work is 20·10 = 200 J, and it equals the change in kinetic energy. Since ½·4·v² = 200, v² = 100 and v = 10 m/s.

quiz.q: A motor uses 600 J of energy in 3 s and does 450 J of useful work. What are its efficiency and useful power?
quiz.e: The efficiency is 450 / 600 = 75%. The useful power is 450 J / 3 s = 150 W. 200 W is the power supplied.
y: If you got 200 W, you divided the supplied 600 J by 3 s. The useful power is 450 J / 3 s.
Efficiency is the ratio of useful work to supplied energy, which is 450/600. Efficiency cannot exceed 100%.
25% is the part that is lost. Efficiency is the share of useful work, 450/600 = 75%.

basit-makineler.title: Simple machines
basit-makineler.summary: Learn about levers, pulleys, inclined planes, the wheel and axle, screws, gears, and efficiency.

cards.p: A simple machine makes work easier by changing the size, the direction, or the distance of a force. The lever, pulley, inclined plane, wheel and axle, screw, and gear are all simple machines.

once.soru: What does the pulley at the top of a flagpole do?

secenekler.yazi: It changes the direction of the force
secenekler.neden: You pull the rope down to raise the flag.
A fixed pulley gives no gain in force.
No machine reduces the work.

cards.h: Gain in force, loss in distance
cards.p: Mechanical advantage is the ratio of the load to the effort (W / F). If it is 4, you lift a 400 N load with 100 N, but you pull 4 times as much rope. So there is no gain in work.

once.soru: A machine lifts a 400 N load with 100 N. How many meters of rope do you pull while the load rises 1 m?

secenekler.neden: If you gain 4 times in force, you lose 4 times in distance, because 100·4 = 400·1.
When the force goes down, the distance goes up, and the work stays the same.
If the distance got shorter, you would gain work, and that never happens.

cards.h: The lever and the balance condition
cards.p: A lever is a bar that turns around a pivot (fulcrum). The perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of the effort is the effort arm, and the distance to the load is the load arm. At balance F·dF = W·dW.

cards.p: The order of the pivot, the load, and the effort sets the type of lever. On a seesaw the pivot is in the middle. On a wheelbarrow the load is in the middle, and the advantage is greater than 1. With tweezers the effort is in the middle, and the advantage is less than 1.

etk.soru: What is in the middle of this lever: the pivot, the load, or the effort?
ogeler: The screw (pivot) is between the handles and the blades.
The rivet (pivot) is between the handles and the jaws.
The wheel is the pivot, the load is in the middle, and you lift at the end.
The nut sits between the hinge and your hand.
The top of the cap is the pivot, and the edge being lifted is in the middle.
Your fingers press between the hinge and the tips.
Your hand squeezes in the middle, and the tips hold the load.
The lower hand is the pivot, and the upper hand applies the effort in the middle.

cards.p: A fixed pulley is attached to the ceiling and does not move with the load. Its advantage is 1, so F = W. Its benefit is that it changes the direction of the force. You pull the rope down to lift the load.

once.soru: With a fixed pulley, how many newtons do you pull with to balance a 200 N load?

secenekler.neden: A fixed pulley gives no gain in force, so F = W.
It is the movable pulley that halves the force.
A fixed pulley does not increase the force. It only changes its direction.

cards.p: A movable pulley rises with the load, and two rope strands carry the load. So F = W/2, and the advantage is 2. The price is that to lift the load by h you pull 2h of rope.

cards.key: If the pulley weighs w, then F = (W + w)/2. If the rope strands are not parallel, the advantage is less than 2.

once.soru: With a weightless movable pulley, how many newtons do you need to lift a 300 N load?

secenekler.neden: Two rope strands share the load, and 300 / 2 = 150 N.
That is true for a fixed pulley.
A movable pulley halves the force.

cards.p: A block and tackle combines fixed and movable pulleys. If n rope strands carry the movable block, then F = W/n. When the load rises by h, you pull n·h of rope.

cards.p: If you push a load up a sloped surface with no friction, F·L = W·h (L is the length of the ramp, h is the height). The longer the ramp, the smaller the force, but the longer the distance.

cards.key: The advantage of an inclined plane is L/h. For the same height, the work W·h does not change.

cards.p: A wheel and axle is a large handle and a small cylinder fixed to the same shaft. At balance F·R = W·r, and the advantage is R/r. A door handle, a steering wheel, and a screwdriver work this way.

cards.key: A well windlass works the same way. In one turn the effort moves 2πR and the load moves 2πr.

once.soru: Why does a thick-handled screwdriver turn a screw more easily than a thin-handled one?

secenekler.neden: For a wheel and axle the advantage is R/r. A larger handle gives the same turning effect with less force.
Weight does not make turning easier.
It is the radius of the handle, not its length, that makes it easier.

cards.p: When simple machines are connected, their advantages multiply. A movable pulley (2) combined with a wheel and axle with R = 4r (4) gives an advantage of 8. So an 800 N load is lifted with 100 N.

once.soru: A pulley with advantage 2 is connected to a wheel and axle with advantage 3. What is the total advantage?

secenekler.neden: For machines connected in a chain the advantages multiply, giving 2 · 3.
Advantages multiply, they do not add.
Advantages do not divide. Each machine reduces the force again.

once.soru: How far does a screw advance in one full turn?

secenekler.neden: In one turn the screw advances by the distance between two neighboring threads.
It takes many turns to drive a screw all the way in.
The circumference is the distance the end of the handle moves. It is not how far the screw advances.

cards.p: The rims of meshing gears move at the same speed. So the number of turns is inversely proportional to the radius, and n₁·r₁ = n₂·r₂. Meshing gears turn in opposite directions.

once.soru: A 20-tooth gear meshes with a 10-tooth gear. When the large gear makes 1 turn, how many turns does the small one make?

secenekler.neden: 1·20 = n·10: the small gear turns twice as fast.
The small gear makes more turns, not fewer.
The numbers of teeth are different, so the numbers of turns are different too.

cards.p: The pedal shares a shaft with the front gear, and the rear gear shares one with the wheel, and the chain links the two. If the front gear has 48 teeth and the rear gear has 16, the wheel makes 3 turns for each turn of the pedal.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><circle cx='225' cy='125' r='52' fill='none' stroke='var(--muted)' stroke-width='2'/><circle cx='225' cy='125' r='2' fill='var(--ink)' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='1.5'/><circle cx='95' cy='125' r='30' fill='var(--c1)' fill-opacity='0.15' stroke='var(--c1)' stroke-width='5' stroke-dasharray='4 3'/><circle cx='225' cy='125' r='10' fill='var(--c4)' fill-opacity='0.2' stroke='var(--c4)' stroke-width='4' stroke-dasharray='3 2'/><line x1='95' y1='94' x2='225' y2='114' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='1.5'/><line x1='95' y1='156' x2='225' y2='136' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='1.5'/><line x1='95' y1='125' x2='73' y2='165' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='3'/><rect x='61' y='163' width='24' height='6' fill='var(--ink)' fill-opacity='0.6' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='1' rx='1'/><circle cx='95' cy='125' r='2.5' fill='var(--ink)' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='1.5'/><text x='160' y='25' font-size='13' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='bold'>Pedal 1 turn → wheel 3 turns</text><text x='160' y='45' font-size='12' fill='var(--acc)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='bold'>48 / 16 = 3</text><text x='137' y='173' font-size='11' fill='var(--c1)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='bold'>48 teeth</text><text x='225' y='153' font-size='11' fill='var(--c4)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='bold'>16 teeth</text><text x='150' y='88' font-size='10' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>chain</text><text x='265' y='70' font-size='10' fill='var(--muted)'>wheel</text></svg>
cards.key: On a hill you shift to a larger rear gear. The wheel then turns less, and pedaling gets easier. Gears linked by a chain turn in the same direction.

cards.p: In a real machine, friction turns part of the work into heat. Efficiency is the useful work divided by the work input, times 100, and it is always below 100%.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><text x='160' y='28' font-size='11' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>Ramp: W = 600 N, h = 1 m, L = 4 m, F = 200 N</text><text x='30' y='62' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' font-weight='bold'>Work input: F·L = 200·4 = 800 J</text><rect x='30' y='72' width='195' height='34' fill='var(--c3)' fill-opacity='0.5' stroke='var(--c3)' stroke-width='1.5'/><rect x='225' y='72' width='65' height='34' fill='var(--c2)' fill-opacity='0.5' stroke='var(--c2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><text x='127' y='94' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='bold'>useful 600 J</text><text x='257' y='94' font-size='11' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='bold'>heat 200 J</text><text x='30' y='128' font-size='12' fill='var(--c3)' font-weight='bold'>Useful work: W·h = 600·1 = 600 J</text><text x='160' y='160' font-size='15' fill='var(--acc)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='bold'>Efficiency = 600 / 800 = 75%</text><text x='160' y='184' font-size='11' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>Without friction F = 150 N would be enough</text></svg>
cards.key: If you apply 200 N to raise a 600 N load by 1 m on a 4 m ramp, the efficiency is 600 J / 800 J = 75%.

cards.p:
• The advantage is W / F, and there is no gain in work.
• For a lever F·dF = W·dW.
• The advantage is 1 for a fixed pulley, 2 for a movable pulley, and n for a block and tackle.
• F·L = W·h for an inclined plane, F·R = W·r for a wheel and axle, and F·2πR = W·a for a screw.
• For gears n₁·r₁ = n₂·r₂.

quiz.q: A 600 N load is lifted with a block and tackle whose movable block is carried by 4 rope strands. If the movable pulleys weigh 40 N in total, what is the smallest force, in N, you must apply to the rope? (no friction)
quiz.e: The weight of the pulleys adds to the load, so F = (W + w) / n = (600 + 40) / 4 = 160 N.

quiz.q: Put each case in the right group by lever type.
ogeler: Lifting a rock with a crowbar
quiz.e: For a crowbar and a balance the pivot is in the middle. For a paper guillotine and for rising onto your toes the load is in the middle. On your toes, the toes are the pivot and the effort is the muscle at the heel. With a broom and a shovel the upper hand is the pivot, and the lower hand applies the effort in the middle.

quiz.q: A 300 N load hangs from one end of a 2 m weightless bar. The pivot is 0.5 m from the load. What is the smallest force, in N, applied perpendicular to the other end that balances the bar?
quiz.e: The effort arm is 2 − 0.5 = 1.5 m. Since F·1.5 = 300·0.5, F = 100 N. The advantage is 1.5 / 0.5 = 3.

quiz.q: Gears K, L, and M mesh in a row and have radii r, 3r, and 2r. If K makes 6 turns clockwise, what does M do?
quiz.e: For gears in contact n·r is constant. Since 6·r = n·2r, n = 3. L turns opposite to K. M turns opposite to L, which is the same direction as K: clockwise.
y: The middle gear L reverses the direction twice. So K and M turn in the same direction, not in opposite directions.
The number of turns is inversely proportional to the radius. If 6·r = n·2r, then n = 3, and the direction is the same as K.
The number of turns is inversely proportional to the radius. So the larger gear M makes fewer turns than K.

momentum.title: Momentum and collisions
momentum.summary: Momentum, impulse, conservation, and elastic or inelastic collisions.

cards.p: Momentum is mass times velocity. It is given by p = m·v, and its unit is kg·m/s. A slow truck is harder to stop than a fast ball, because its mass is large and so its momentum is large too.

momentum</text></svg>
cards.key: Momentum is p = m·v, and its unit is kg·m/s. Being fast does not by itself mean a large momentum.

cards.p: Momentum points the same way as the velocity. Choose one direction as + and count the opposite as −. Momenta add as vectors. Two objects with equal and opposite momenta have a total momentum of zero.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><defs><marker id='mom-3' viewBox='0 0 10 10' refX='9' refY='5' markerWidth='5' markerHeight='5' orient='auto'><path d='M0,0 L10,5 L0,10 z' fill='var(--c1)'/></marker><marker id='mom-4' viewBox='0 0 10 10' refX='9' refY='5' markerWidth='5' markerHeight='5' orient='auto'><path d='M0,0 L10,5 L0,10 z' fill='var(--c2)'/></marker></defs><text x='160' y='28' font-size='12' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>right: +, left: −</text><rect x='50' y='65' width='40' height='34' rx='3' fill='var(--c1)' fill-opacity='0.25' stroke='var(--c1)' stroke-width='1.5'/><text x='70' y='87' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>2 kg</text><line x1='92' y1='82' x2='142' y2='82' stroke='var(--c1)' stroke-width='2.5' marker-end='url(#mom-3)'/><text x='117' y='72' font-size='12' fill='var(--c1)' text-anchor='middle'>3 m/s</text><rect x='230' y='65' width='40' height='34' rx='3' fill='var(--c2)' fill-opacity='0.25' stroke='var(--c2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><text x='250' y='87' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>3 kg</text><line x1='228' y1='82' x2='178' y2='82' stroke='var(--c2)' stroke-width='2.5' marker-end='url(#mom-4)'/><text x='203' y='72' font-size='12' fill='var(--c2)' text-anchor='middle'>2 m/s</text><text x='70' y='125' font-size='13' fill='var(--c1)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='bold'>p₁ = +6 kg·m/s</text><text x='250' y='125' font-size='13' fill='var(--c2)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='bold'>p₂ = −6 kg·m/s</text><text x='160' y='160' font-size='14' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='bold'>total: (+6) + (−6) = 0</text><text x='160' y='186' font-size='12' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>both are moving, yet the total momentum is zero</text></svg>
cards.key: Choose the + direction before you start a calculation. Velocity and momentum in the opposite direction get a minus sign.

once.soru: Two 1 kg balls move toward each other at 3 m/s. What is the total momentum, in kg·m/s?

secenekler.neden: The momenta point in opposite directions. +3 and −3 add up to zero.
Opposite momenta do not add up, they cancel.
The two balls carry momenta of equal size in opposite directions.

cards.p: A net force acting for a time gives an impulse, I = F·Δt. The impulse equals the change in momentum (I = Δp). Its unit is N·s, which is the same as kg·m/s.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><defs><marker id='mom-5' viewBox='0 0 10 10' refX='9' refY='5' markerWidth='5' markerHeight='5' orient='auto'><path d='M0,0 L10,5 L0,10 z' fill='var(--c2)'/></marker><marker id='mom-6' viewBox='0 0 10 10' refX='9' refY='5' markerWidth='5' markerHeight='5' orient='auto'><path d='M0,0 L10,5 L0,10 z' fill='var(--c3)'/></marker></defs><text x='160' y='28' font-size='12' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>0.5 kg ball, frictionless surface</text><circle cx='45' cy='85' r='14' fill='var(--c5)' fill-opacity='0.3' stroke='var(--c5)' stroke-width='1.5'/><text x='45' y='125' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>before: v = 0</text><line x1='70' y1='85' x2='140' y2='85' stroke='var(--c2)' stroke-width='3' marker-end='url(#mom-5)'/><text x='105' y='72' font-size='12' fill='var(--c2)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='bold'>F = 50 N</text><text x='105' y='106' font-size='12' fill='var(--c2)' text-anchor='middle'>Δt = 0.1 s</text><circle cx='185' cy='85' r='14' fill='var(--c5)' fill-opacity='0.3' stroke='var(--c5)' stroke-width='1.5'/><line x1='205' y1='85' x2='275' y2='85' stroke='var(--c3)' stroke-width='2.5' marker-end='url(#mom-6)'/><text x='240' y='72' font-size='12' fill='var(--c3)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='bold'>10 m/s</text><text x='210' y='125' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>after: v = 10 m/s</text><line x1='20' y1='140' x2='300' y2='140' stroke='var(--line)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='160' y='162' font-size='13' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='bold'>I = F·Δt = 50 × 0.1 = 5 N·s</text><text x='160' y='186' font-size='13' fill='var(--acc)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='bold'>Δp = 0.5 × 10 − 0 = 5 kg·m/s</text></svg>
cards.key: Impulse is a vector too, and it points along the net force, which is the direction of Δp. If the force changes, use the average force.

once.soru: A 50 N force acts on a ball at rest for 0.1 s. What is its momentum, in kg·m/s?

secenekler.neden: I = F·Δt = 50·0.1 = 5 N·s, and the change in momentum equals this.
The force is multiplied by the time, not divided.
Force alone is not momentum. It has to be multiplied by the time.

cards.h: Area under the F–t graph = impulse
cards.p: If the force changes, the impulse is the area under the force–time graph. Area below the axis is impulse in the opposite direction, and it is subtracted. For a constant force the area is a rectangle equal to F·Δt.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><defs><marker id='mom-7' viewBox='0 0 10 10' refX='9' refY='5' markerWidth='5' markerHeight='5' orient='auto'><path d='M0,0 L10,5 L0,10 z' fill='var(--ink)'/></marker></defs><polygon points='40,160 110,70 180,70 250,160' fill='var(--acc)' fill-opacity='0.2' stroke='var(--acc)' stroke-width='2.5'/><line x1='40' y1='160' x2='295' y2='160' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='1.5' marker-end='url(#mom-7)'/><line x1='40' y1='160' x2='40' y2='22' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='1.5' marker-end='url(#mom-7)'/><text x='48' y='26' font-size='12' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='start'>F (N)</text><text x='300' y='190' font-size='12' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='end'>t (s)</text><line x1='40' y1='70' x2='110' y2='70' stroke='var(--muted)' stroke-width='1' stroke-dasharray='4 3'/><text x='34' y='74' font-size='12' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='end'>20</text><text x='110' y='176' font-size='12' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>2</text><text x='180' y='176' font-size='12' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>4</text><text x='250' y='176' font-size='12' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>6</text><text x='145' y='120' font-size='13' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='bold'>area = impulse</text><text x='145' y='140' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>20 + 40 + 20 = 80 N·s</text><text x='300' y='40' font-size='13' fill='var(--acc)' text-anchor='end' font-weight='bold'>I = Δp = 80 N·s</text></svg>
cards.key: The area under a force–time graph gives the impulse, which is Δp. The area under a force–extension graph is work. Do not mix them up.

once.soru: On an F–t graph the force rises steadily from 0 to 10 N over 4 s. What is the impulse, in N·s?

secenekler.neden: The area is a triangle, and ½ · 4 · 10 = 20 N·s.
That would be right for a rectangle. But the force is not 10 N the whole time.
Impulse is the area, not the force. Take the time into account too.

cards.p: The Δp needed to stop is fixed. Since F = Δp / Δt, a longer time means a smaller force. That is why an airbag, helmet foam, and bending your knees protect you.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><defs><marker id='mom-8' viewBox='0 0 10 10' refX='9' refY='5' markerWidth='5' markerHeight='5' orient='auto'><path d='M0,0 L10,5 L0,10 z' fill='var(--ink)'/></marker></defs><polygon points='50,170 65,50 80,170' fill='var(--c2)' fill-opacity='0.25' stroke='var(--c2)' stroke-width='2'/><polygon points='110,170 155,130 200,170' fill='var(--c3)' fill-opacity='0.25' stroke='var(--c3)' stroke-width='2'/><line x1='40' y1='170' x2='300' y2='170' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='1.5' marker-end='url(#mom-8)'/><line x1='40' y1='170' x2='40' y2='22' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='1.5' marker-end='url(#mom-8)'/><text x='48' y='26' font-size='12' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='start'>F</text><text x='300' y='190' font-size='12' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='end'>t</text><text x='74' y='64' font-size='12' fill='var(--c2)' text-anchor='start' font-weight='bold'>hard ground</text><text x='170' y='128' font-size='12' fill='var(--c3)' text-anchor='start' font-weight='bold'>airbag</text><text x='300' y='30' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='end'>equal areas → same Δp</text><text x='300' y='50' font-size='12' fill='var(--c2)' text-anchor='end'>short Δt → large F</text><text x='300' y='70' font-size='12' fill='var(--c3)' text-anchor='end'>long Δt → small F</text></svg>
cards.key: An airbag does not reduce the impulse (Δp). It makes the time longer and so reduces the force.

cards.h: The momentum form of the second law
cards.p: The general form of the second law is Fnet = Δp / Δt. If the mass is constant, Δp = m·Δv, and this gives F = m·a. If the net force is zero, the momentum does not change.

cards.key: F = m·a is the form that F = Δp/Δt takes when the mass is constant.

once.soru: If the net force on an object is zero, what happens to its momentum?

secenekler.neden: Since Fnet = Δp/Δt, if the force is zero then Δp is zero too.
For it to decrease, there must be a net force opposing the motion.
The momentum of a moving object is conserved when there is no force.

cards.h: A ball bouncing off a wall
cards.p: When the direction changes, watch the sign. For a ball that hits a wall at speed v and bounces back at the same speed, Δp = m(−v) − m(v) = −2mv. If the ball stuck, Δp would be only mv.

cards.p: If the external forces add up to zero, the total momentum of a system is conserved. The forces that colliding objects exert on each other are an action–reaction pair. These equal and opposite impulses cancel.

cards.key: The momentum one object gains, the other loses. Because a collision is brief, external forces such as friction are usually neglected.

once.soru: Two skaters at rest on an ice rink push each other apart. What happens to their total momentum?

secenekler.neden: There is no external force. So the total momentum, zero at the start, stays zero.
Both of them move, but their momenta point in opposite directions.
The momentum was already zero at the start, and it is conserved.

cards.p: In an elastic collision both momentum and kinetic energy are conserved. Billiard balls come close to this. The swap of velocities you just saw happens only if the masses are equal.

girdiler.etiket: Mass of the object at rest

cards.p: If a system at rest breaks apart, the total momentum stays zero. The pieces fly apart with equal and opposite momenta. The recoil of a rifle and a rocket work this way.

cards.key: A rocket does not need air. In an explosion the kinetic energy increases, and this energy comes from the fuel or from a spring. Since KE = p²/2m, the lighter piece has the larger kinetic energy.

cards.h: Velocity of the center of mass
cards.p: The velocity of the center of mass is vCM = Σp / Σm. With no external force, vCM stays constant. When a firework explodes in the air, the center of mass of its pieces keeps following the old path.
cards.key: The center of mass is the average position that behaves as if all the mass were gathered at one point.

once.soru: A firework flying through the air explodes. How does the center of mass of the pieces move?

secenekler.yazi: It continues on its old path
secenekler.neden: The explosion is an internal event. It does not change the motion of the center of mass.
An explosion does not destroy momentum.
The pieces scatter, but the center of mass follows the old path.

cards.p: In a collision in a plane, momentum is conserved in each component separately. If the incoming ball moves only in the x direction, then after the collision the y momenta of the two balls are equal and opposite.

cards.key: Add the momentum components, not the speeds. Write separate equations for x and y.

once.soru: In billiards the cue ball comes in along x and hits a ball at rest. What is the total y momentum after the collision?

secenekler.neden: There was no momentum in the y direction at the start. Each component is conserved separately.

secenekler.yazi: The same as the cue ball's
secenekler.neden: The momentum in the x direction is conserved, and the total in the y direction stays zero.
Without an external force, y momentum cannot appear.

cards.p:
• Momentum p = m·v is a vector, and its unit is kg·m/s.
• Impulse is I = F·Δt = Δp, and it equals the area under the force–time graph.
• For the same Δp, a longer time means a smaller force.
• With no external force, the total momentum is conserved.
• In an elastic collision KE is conserved too. In other collisions it decreases, and in an explosion it increases.

quiz.q: On a frictionless level track, a 3 kg cart moving at 4 m/s hits a 1 kg cart at rest and sticks to it. What is their common velocity, in m/s?
quiz.e: Momentum is conserved: 3·4 + 1·0 = (3 + 1)·v. This gives v = 12 / 4 = 3 m/s.

quiz.q: What happens to the total kinetic energy of the system in each event?
quiz.e: In an elastic collision kinetic energy is conserved. For vehicles that stick together or get crushed, part of the kinetic energy turns into heat, sound, and deformation. In an explosion or a shot, pieces at rest start to move. The energy comes from the fuel, and the kinetic energy increases.

quiz.q: The net force on a 2 kg object at rest rises steadily from 0 to 50 N in 0.2 s, then falls steadily back to zero in the next 0.2 s. What is the object's final speed, in m/s?
quiz.e: The force–time graph is a triangle, and the impulse is ½ · 0.4 · 50 = 10 N·s. This equals Δp. So v = 10 / 2 = 5 m/s.

quiz.q: A 0.5 kg ball hits a wall head-on at 6 m/s and bounces back at 4 m/s. The contact lasts 0.05 s. What is the average force, in N, that the wall exerts on the ball?
quiz.e: Taking the backward direction as −, Δp = 0.5·(−4) − 0.5·6 = −5 kg·m/s, with a magnitude of 5 N·s. The force is F = 5 / 0.05 = 100 N. Subtracting the speeds (6 − 4) is wrong, because the direction changed.

tork-denge.title: Torque, equilibrium, and center of mass
tork-denge.summary: How does a force cause rotation, and when does an object stay balanced or tip over?

cards.p: The turning effect of a force is called torque, given by τ = F·d. Here d is the perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of the force, and it is called the lever arm. With a longer arm, less force is enough.

cards.key: Torque is also called the moment of a force. For the same torque, a longer lever arm needs less force (F = τ / d).

cards.p: If the force makes an angle θ with r, the lever arm is d = r·sinθ, and τ = F·r·sinθ. The component perpendicular to r does the turning. sin90° = 1 and sin0° = 0.

once.soru: A torque of 30 N·m clockwise and 20 N·m counterclockwise act on a bar. What is the net torque, in N·m?

secenekler.neden: Opposite torques are subtracted: 30 − 20 = 10 N·m, clockwise.
Opposite torques do not add up, they are subtracted.
If the torques were equal, the total would be zero. But 30 and 20 are not equal.

cards.h: Unit: N·m, but not the joule
cards.p: The unit of torque is the N·m. The joule is also N·m, but in work the force is multiplied by the distance along the same line, and in torque by the perpendicular distance. So torque is not written in joules.

once.soru: Which is the unit of torque?

secenekler.neden: Torque is force times perpendicular distance. Its unit is the newton times the meter.
The joule is for work and energy. Torque is written in N·m.
The newton is the unit of force. In torque the force is multiplied by a distance.

cards.p: To find the tension in a rope holding a hinged bar, take torques about the hinge, because the torque of the hinge force is zero. The torque of the rope is T·L·sinα, and the torque of the bar is W·L/2.

cards.key: The tension depends on the angle the rope makes with the bar. The smaller the angle, the larger T.

once.soru: The end of a 100 N horizontal bar hinged to a wall is held by a rope at 30° to the bar. What is the tension in the rope, in N?

secenekler.neden: About the hinge, T·L·sin30° = 100·L/2. This gives T = 100 N.
The weight acts at the middle, but the rope pulls at an angle. So sin30° = 0.5 comes into it.
The weight of the bar acts at its middle, not at its end.

cards.h: Center of mass and center of gravity
cards.p: The center of mass is the point where an object behaves as if all its mass were there. In uniform gravity the weight also acts at this point, which is called the center of gravity. For a ring this point is in empty space.

once.soru: Where is the center of mass of a uniform ring?

secenekler.neden: A ring is symmetric. Its center of mass is at the geometric center, even though there is no material there.
Every point of the ring is symmetric, and no point stands out.

secenekler.yazi: It has no center of mass
secenekler.neden: Every object has a center of mass.

cards.h: Center of mass of a composite object
cards.p: For an object made of parts, the center of mass is xCM = Σm·x / Σm. The center of mass is closer to the heavier part. A part that has been removed counts as a negative mass.

cards.h: Base of support and tipping over
cards.p: If the vertical line down from the center of gravity falls inside the base of support, the object does not tip over. If it falls outside, the object tips. A low center of gravity and a wide base make tipping harder.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><defs><marker id='tork-17' viewBox='0 0 10 10' refX='9' refY='5' markerWidth='9' markerHeight='9' markerUnits='userSpaceOnUse' orient='auto'><path d='M0,0 L10,5 L0,10 z' fill='var(--ink)'/></marker></defs><line x1='10.0' y1='150.0' x2='310.0' y2='150.0' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='2'/><g transform='rotate(15,100,150)'><rect x='60' y='70' width='40' height='80' fill='var(--c3)' fill-opacity='0.2' stroke='var(--c3)' stroke-width='1.5'/></g><circle cx='91.0' cy='106.2' r='4' fill='var(--ink)'/><line x1='91.0' y1='106.2' x2='91.0' y2='150.0' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='1.5' stroke-dasharray='4 3' marker-end='url(#tork-17)'/><circle cx='100' cy='150' r='3' fill='var(--c4)'/><g transform='rotate(40,240,150)'><rect x='200' y='70' width='40' height='80' fill='var(--c2)' fill-opacity='0.2' stroke='var(--c2)' stroke-width='1.5'/></g><circle cx='250.4' cy='106.5' r='4' fill='var(--ink)'/><line x1='250.4' y1='106.5' x2='250.4' y2='150.0' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='1.5' stroke-dasharray='4 3' marker-end='url(#tork-17)'/><circle cx='240' cy='150' r='3' fill='var(--c4)'/><text x='80.0' y='172.0' font-size='12' fill='var(--c3)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='bold'>line inside the base</text><text x='80.0' y='188.0' font-size='11' fill='var(--c3)' text-anchor='middle'>returns</text><text x='235.0' y='172.0' font-size='12' fill='var(--c2)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='bold'>line outside the base</text><text x='235.0' y='188.0' font-size='11' fill='var(--c2)' text-anchor='middle'>tips over</text><text x='160.0' y='22.0' font-size='12' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>vertical line from the center of gravity</text></svg>
cards.key: The tipping limit is the moment the vertical line through the center of gravity passes exactly through the edge of the base. That is why race cars are low.

cards.p: A box on an incline slides when tanα > μs and tips when tanα > b/h (b is the base, h is the height). As the angle grows, whichever limit is reached first happens.
cards.key: If μs < b/h, the box slides without tipping; if μs > b/h, it tips without sliding.

once.soru: You put a low box with a wide base on an icy ramp. If the ramp slowly gets steeper, what does the box do first?

secenekler.neden: On ice there is very little friction, so the sliding limit is reached early. For a low box to tip, the ramp would have to be very steep.
A low box has a low center of gravity. The ramp would have to get very steep for it to tip.
There is little friction on ice. The box starts to move as soon as the ramp gets a bit steeper.

cards.p: If an object returns after a small push, its equilibrium is stable. If it moves away, it is unstable. If it stays in its new place, it is neutral. In stable equilibrium the center of gravity is at its lowest.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><path d='M15,80 Q55,150 95,80' fill='none' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='2'/><circle cx='55' cy='105' r='10' fill='var(--c3)' fill-opacity='0.5' stroke='var(--c3)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M120,130 Q160,70 200,130' fill='none' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='2'/><circle cx='160' cy='90' r='10' fill='var(--c2)' fill-opacity='0.5' stroke='var(--c2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><line x1='225.0' y1='115.0' x2='305.0' y2='115.0' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='2'/><circle cx='265' cy='105' r='10' fill='var(--c1)' fill-opacity='0.5' stroke='var(--c1)' stroke-width='1.5'/><text x='55.0' y='150.0' font-size='13' fill='var(--c3)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='bold'>stable</text><text x='55.0' y='167.0' font-size='11' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>returns</text><text x='55.0' y='183.0' font-size='10' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>hanging pendulum</text><text x='160.0' y='150.0' font-size='13' fill='var(--c2)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='bold'>unstable</text><text x='160.0' y='167.0' font-size='11' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>moves away</text><text x='160.0' y='183.0' font-size='10' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>inverted pendulum</text><text x='265.0' y='150.0' font-size='13' fill='var(--c1)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='bold'>neutral</text><text x='265.0' y='167.0' font-size='11' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>stays in new place</text><text x='265.0' y='183.0' font-size='10' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>ball on flat ground</text><text x='160.0' y='26.0' font-size='13' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='bold'>push the ball a little: what happens?</text></svg>
cards.key: A ball in a hollow is in stable equilibrium, a ball on a hilltop is unstable, and a ball on flat ground is neutral. After a push, the center of gravity rises in the stable case and drops in the unstable case.

etk.soru: What happens after a small push? Choose the type of equilibrium.
ogeler: Ball at the bottom of a hollow
Ruler hung from its top end
When pushed, the center of gravity rises, and the ruler swings back.
Ball on top of a hill
When pushed, the center of gravity drops, and the pencil falls.
As it rolls, the center of gravity stays at the same height.
Wheel mounted on an axle at its center
As it turns, the center of gravity does not move.

once.soru: You give a small push to a ball at the bottom of a hollow. What happens?

secenekler.neden: When pushed, the ball rises. Its weight pulls it back to the lowest point.
A ball on a hilltop would move away. A ball in a hollow cannot climb out.

secenekler.yazi: It stays in its new place
secenekler.neden: A ball on flat ground would do that. In a hollow the ground rises toward the edges.

cards.p:
• Torque is τ = F·d = F·r·sinθ, and its unit is N·m. Its direction is clockwise or counterclockwise.
• Equilibrium needs both ΣF = 0 and Στ = 0.
• The weight of a uniform bar acts at its middle.
• The center of mass is xCM = Σm·x / Σm.
• If the vertical line falls outside the base, the object tips over.

quiz.q: A 50 N force is applied to the end of a 0.4 m wrench at an angle of 30° to the wrench. What is the torque about the nut, in N·m?
quiz.e: τ = F·r·sinθ = 50·0.4·0.5 = 10 N·m. If the force were perpendicular to the wrench, the torque would be 20 N·m.

quiz.q: What happens after a small push? Choose the type of equilibrium for each object.
ogeler: Picture hung on a nail from its top
Broom balanced upright on a finger
Ruler on an axle through its center of mass
quiz.e: When a cone on its base or a hanging picture is pushed, the center of gravity rises and the object returns. These are in stable equilibrium. When a cone on its tip or an upright broom is pushed, the center of gravity drops and the object falls. These are in unstable equilibrium. When a cone on its side rolls or a ruler on an axle turns, the height of the center of gravity does not change. These are in neutral equilibrium.

quiz.q: A force is applied to a hinged bar. r is the distance from the hinge to the point where the force acts. Put the torques in order from smallest to largest.
ogeler: 20 N, r = 0.5 m, line of action through the hinge
20 N, r = 0.8 m, at 30° to the bar
20 N, r = 0.5 m, perpendicular to the bar
30 N, r = 0.6 m, perpendicular to the bar
quiz.e: Use τ = F·r·sinθ. For the force whose line passes through the hinge, τ = 0. The others are 20·0.8·0.5 = 8, 20·0.5 = 10, and 30·0.6 = 18 N·m.

quiz.q: A 6 m uniform bar weighing 120 N is supported at its ends A and B. A 300 N load is 2 m from end A. What force, in N, does support B exert on the bar?
quiz.e: Taking torques about A, N<sub>B</sub>·6 = 120·3 + 300·2 = 960, so N<sub>B</sub> = 160 N. From ΣF = 0, N<sub>A</sub> = 420 − 160 = 260 N.

madde-ozellikleri.title: Matter and its properties
madde-ozellikleri.summary: Learn about mass, volume, density, strength, adhesion, and capillary action.

cards.p: Anything that has mass and volume is matter. Mass, volume, and inertia are common properties found in all matter. Density, melting point, and conductivity are distinguishing properties that identify a substance.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><rect x='14' y='14' width='140' height='172' rx='8' fill='var(--c1)' fill-opacity='0.15' stroke='var(--c1)' stroke-width='1.5'/><text x='84' y='36' font-size='13' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>Common</text><text x='84' y='62' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>mass</text><text x='84' y='86' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>volume</text><text x='84' y='110' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>inertia</text><text x='84' y='134' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>made of particles</text><text x='84' y='170' font-size='10' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>in all matter</text><rect x='166' y='14' width='140' height='172' rx='8' fill='var(--acc)' fill-opacity='0.15' stroke='var(--acc)' stroke-width='1.5'/><text x='236' y='36' font-size='13' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>Distinguishing</text><text x='236' y='62' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>density</text><text x='236' y='84' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>melting point</text><text x='236' y='106' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>elasticity</text><text x='236' y='128' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>conductivity</text><text x='236' y='150' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>solubility</text><text x='236' y='170' font-size='10' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>identify a substance</text></svg>

once.soru: Which one is found in all matter?

secenekler.neden: All matter has mass and volume. So mass does not identify a substance, and it is a common property.
A magnet attracts iron but not wood. So not all matter is magnetic.
Copper conducts electricity, and plastic does not. So conductivity changes from one substance to another.

cards.key: Inertia is the tendency of an object to keep its state of motion. You will see the details in Newton's laws.

cards.p: Mass is the amount of matter. It is measured with an equal-arm balance and does not change from place to place. Volume is the space that matter takes up. 1 L = 1 dm³ and 1 mL = 1 cm³.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><path d='M60 60 H140 M100 60 V150 M70 150 H130' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='2' fill='none'/><path d='M60 60 l-14 40 h28 z M140 60 l-14 40 h28 z' fill='var(--panel)' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='1.5'/><circle cx='60' cy='92' r='8' fill='var(--c4)' fill-opacity='0.5'/><rect x='131' y='88' width='18' height='10' fill='var(--muted)'/><text x='100' y='178' font-size='11' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>equal-arm balance: mass (kg)</text><path d='M220 40 V160 H270 V40' fill='none' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='2'/><rect x='221' y='95' width='48' height='64' fill='var(--c1)' fill-opacity='0.25'/><path d='M221 80 h48' stroke='var(--c1)' stroke-dasharray='3 3'/><circle cx='245' cy='140' r='12' fill='var(--c4)' fill-opacity='0.5' stroke='var(--ink)'/><path d='M270 60 h8' stroke='var(--muted)'/><path d='M270 80 h8' stroke='var(--muted)'/><path d='M270 100 h8' stroke='var(--muted)'/><path d='M270 120 h8' stroke='var(--muted)'/><path d='M270 140 h8' stroke='var(--muted)'/><text x='245' y='178' font-size='11' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>displaced water = volume</text><text x='290' y='98' font-size='14' fill='var(--c1)' text-anchor='middle'>↑</text></svg>
cards.key: Mass and weight are not the same thing. On the Moon your mass stays the same, but your weight (the force of gravity on you) is smaller.

cards.p: The mass of a unit volume is called density, given by ρ = m / V (g/cm³). A nail and a door made of iron have the same density. So density identifies a substance.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><text x='160' y='58' font-size='30' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='800'>ρ = m / V</text><text x='160' y='84' font-size='12' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>density = mass / volume</text><rect x='20' y='110' width='84' height='64' rx='8' fill='var(--c1)' fill-opacity='0.15' stroke='var(--c1)' stroke-width='1.5'/><text x='62' y='136' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>water</text><text x='62' y='156' font-size='12' fill='var(--acc)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>1 g/cm³</text><rect x='118' y='110' width='84' height='64' rx='8' fill='var(--c4)' fill-opacity='0.15' stroke='var(--c4)' stroke-width='1.5'/><text x='160' y='136' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>aluminum</text><text x='160' y='156' font-size='12' fill='var(--acc)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>2.7 g/cm³</text><rect x='216' y='110' width='84' height='64' rx='8' fill='var(--c5)' fill-opacity='0.15' stroke='var(--c5)' stroke-width='1.5'/><text x='258' y='136' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>iron</text><text x='258' y='156' font-size='12' fill='var(--acc)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>7.9 g/cm³</text></svg>
cards.key: The density of water is 1 g/cm³, which is 1000 kg/m³.

etk.soru: Change the mass and the volume. How does the density change? The density of water is 1 g/cm³.
yorum: This substance is less dense than water. An object made of it floats in water.
The density of this substance equals that of water. The object stays suspended in water.
This substance is denser than water. An object made of it sinks in water.

cards.p: The mass–volume graph of a substance is a straight line through the origin. The slope of the line is m/V, which is the density. The steeper the line, the denser the substance.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><path d='M50 170 H290 M50 170 V20' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='1.5'/><text x='290' y='188' font-size='12' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='end'>V</text><text x='40' y='26' font-size='12' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='end'>m</text><path d='M50 170 L170 30' stroke='var(--c2)' stroke-width='2.5'/><path d='M50 170 L280 80' stroke='var(--c1)' stroke-width='2.5'/><text x='176' y='30' font-size='11' fill='var(--c2)' text-anchor='start'>X: steep, high density</text><text x='210' y='72' font-size='11' fill='var(--c1)' text-anchor='start'>Y: shallow, low</text><path d='M50 170 L215 45' stroke='var(--c3)' stroke-width='2' stroke-dasharray='6 4'/><text x='220' y='48' font-size='11' fill='var(--c3)' text-anchor='start'>mixture</text><text x='170' y='160' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>slope = m / V = density</text></svg>
cards.key: If the axes are swapped (a V–m graph), the slope is 1/ρ. A density–volume graph is a horizontal line.

cards.p: The density of a mixture is ρ = mtotal / Vfinal. The result lies between the two densities and is closer to that of the substance with more volume. For equal volumes the density of the mixture is (ρ₁ + ρ₂) / 2.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><rect x='20' y='30' width='70' height='70' rx='8' fill='var(--c1)' fill-opacity='0.15' stroke='var(--c1)' stroke-width='1.5'/><text x='55' y='62' font-size='13' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>ρ₁</text><text x='55' y='80' font-size='10' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>V₁, m₁</text><text x='105' y='70' font-size='18' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>+</text><rect x='120' y='30' width='70' height='70' rx='8' fill='var(--c4)' fill-opacity='0.15' stroke='var(--c4)' stroke-width='1.5'/><text x='155' y='62' font-size='13' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>ρ₂</text><text x='155' y='80' font-size='10' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>V₂, m₂</text><text x='205' y='70' font-size='18' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>=</text><rect x='220' y='30' width='80' height='70' rx='8' fill='var(--acc)' fill-opacity='0.15' stroke='var(--acc)' stroke-width='1.5'/><text x='260' y='70' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>ρ mixture</text><text x='160' y='130' font-size='15' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>ρ = m total / V final</text><text x='160' y='158' font-size='12' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>if volume is unchanged: V final = V₁ + V₂</text><text x='160' y='180' font-size='12' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>then for equal volumes: (ρ₁ + ρ₂) / 2</text></svg>
cards.key: When water and alcohol mix, the volume shrinks a little. So V₁ + V₂ is only an approximation.

cards.p: Matter expands when heated. Its mass stays the same, its volume increases, and its density decreases. Water is an exception, because it is densest at 4 °C.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><path d='M60 30 V170 H260' fill='none' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M60 150 Q130 30 150 30 Q170 30 255 120' fill='none' stroke='var(--c1)' stroke-width='2.5'/><path d='M150 30 V170' stroke='var(--line)' stroke-dasharray='3 3'/><text x='150' y='186' font-size='12' fill='var(--acc)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>4 °C</text><text x='40' y='40' font-size='12' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>ρ</text><text x='258' y='186' font-size='11' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='end'>temperature</text><text x='196' y='30' font-size='11' fill='var(--c1)' text-anchor='start'>water is densest</text><text x='196' y='44' font-size='11' fill='var(--c1)' text-anchor='start'>at 4 °C</text></svg>

once.soru: A metal ball expands a little when heated. What happens to its density?

secenekler.neden: The mass stays the same and the volume increases. So ρ = m / V gets smaller.
The mass does not increase, the volume does. When the divisor grows, the result shrinks.
The volume changed. Since the mass stayed the same, the ratio changes too.

cards.p: If all the dimensions of an object double, its cross-sectional area becomes 4 times larger and its weight 8 times larger. So its strength is cut in half. That is why an elephant has thick legs.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><rect x='40' y='120' width='30' height='30' fill='var(--c1)' fill-opacity='0.25' stroke='var(--c1)' stroke-width='1.5'/><rect x='150' y='90' width='60' height='60' fill='var(--c4)' fill-opacity='0.25' stroke='var(--c4)' stroke-width='1.5'/><text x='55' y='170' font-size='11' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>side 1</text><text x='180' y='170' font-size='11' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>side 2</text><g font-size='11' fill='var(--ink)'><text x='240' y='60'>area: ×4</text><text x='240' y='80'>volume: ×8</text><text x='240' y='100'>strength:</text><text x='240' y='118' fill='var(--c2)' font-weight='700'>halved</text></g><text x='160' y='30' font-size='13' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>strength = cross-sectional area / volume</text></svg>
cards.key: If the dimensions grow k times, the strength drops to 1/k.

once.soru: You double all the sides of a cube. How many times larger does its volume become?

secenekler.neden: Volume is the product of three sides, so it grows 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 times. The cross-sectional area grows only 2 × 2 = 4 times.
Each side doubles, but volume multiplies three sides.
4 times is the growth of the cross-sectional area. For volume the third side is multiplied in too.

cards.p: The attraction between particles of the same kind is called cohesion, and between particles of different kinds adhesion. Water adheres strongly to glass, so it wets the glass. Mercury does not wet glass.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><path d='M60 40 V160 H120 V40' fill='none' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='2'/><path d='M61 90 Q90 110 119 90 V159 H61 Z' fill='var(--c1)' fill-opacity='0.3'/><path d='M200 40 V160 H260 V40' fill='none' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='2'/><path d='M201 104 Q230 80 259 104 V159 H201 Z' fill='var(--muted)' fill-opacity='0.4'/><text x='90' y='180' font-size='11' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>water: concave surface</text><text x='230' y='180' font-size='11' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>mercury: convex surface</text><text x='90' y='28' font-size='11' fill='var(--c1)' text-anchor='middle'>adhesion > cohesion</text><text x='230' y='28' font-size='11' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>cohesion > adhesion</text></svg>

cards.p: Particles at the surface are pulled only from below and from the sides. So the surface behaves like a stretched film. This is called surface tension. Heat and detergent reduce surface tension.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><path d='M20 110 Q160 104 300 110' fill='none' stroke='var(--c1)' stroke-width='2'/><rect x='20' y='111' width='280' height='70' fill='var(--c1)' fill-opacity='0.12'/><path d='M120 100 Q160 112 200 100' fill='none' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='2'/><path d='M140 96 l-30 -40 M180 96 l30 -40 M150 100 l-20 -50 M170 100 l20 -50' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='1.5'/><ellipse cx='160' cy='92' rx='14' ry='6' fill='var(--ink)'/><text x='160' y='30' font-size='13' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>the water surface acts like a stretched film</text><text x='160' y='150' font-size='12' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>a water strider does not sink</text></svg>

once.soru: A water strider walks on water without sinking. What makes this possible?

secenekler.yazi: The stretched surface of the water
secenekler.neden: The water particles at the surface hold each other tightly. The surface carries the insect like a thin film.
The insect walks on still water too, so no current is needed.
Every living thing has mass. It is the surface of the water that carries the insect.

cards.p:
• Mass, volume, and inertia are common properties. Density is a distinguishing property.
• Density is ρ = m / V, and it equals the slope of the mass–volume graph.
• For a mixture ρ = mtotal / Vfinal.
• If the size grows k times, the strength drops to 1/k.
• Cohesion and adhesion explain surface tension and capillary action.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><rect x='14' y='20' width='140' height='48' rx='8' fill='var(--c1)' fill-opacity='0.15' stroke='var(--c1)' stroke-width='1.5'/><text x='84' y='49' font-size='13' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>ρ = m / V</text><rect x='166' y='20' width='140' height='48' rx='8' fill='var(--acc)' fill-opacity='0.15' stroke='var(--acc)' stroke-width='1.5'/><text x='236' y='49' font-size='13' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>mixture: m / V final</text><rect x='14' y='80' width='140' height='48' rx='8' fill='var(--c4)' fill-opacity='0.15' stroke='var(--c4)' stroke-width='1.5'/><text x='84' y='109' font-size='13' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>strength 1/k</text><rect x='166' y='80' width='140' height='48' rx='8' fill='var(--c3)' fill-opacity='0.15' stroke='var(--c3)' stroke-width='1.5'/><text x='236' y='109' font-size='13' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>cohesion/adhesion</text><rect x='14' y='140' width='140' height='48' rx='8' fill='var(--c5)' fill-opacity='0.15' stroke='var(--c5)' stroke-width='1.5'/><text x='84' y='169' font-size='13' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>surface tension</text><rect x='166' y='140' width='140' height='48' rx='8' fill='var(--c2)' fill-opacity='0.15' stroke='var(--c2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><text x='236' y='169' font-size='13' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>capillary action</text></svg>

quiz.q: Put each property in the right group.
quiz.e: Mass, volume, inertia, and being made of particles are found in all matter. Density, melting and boiling points, and conductivity change from one substance to another and identify it.

quiz.q: 200 cm³ of a liquid with density 1 g/cm³ is mixed with 100 cm³ of a liquid with density 4 g/cm³. If the volume does not change on mixing, what is the density of the mixture, in g/cm³?
quiz.e: The total mass is 200·1 + 100·4 = 600 g, and the final volume is 300 cm³. The density is 600 / 300 = 2 g/cm³. The result is closer to the density of the liquid with more volume.

quiz.q: Match each event with the idea that explains it.
ciftler: A paper towel soaking up water
quiz.e: The stretched surface carries the water strider. Water rising in thin channels is called capillary action. Water wets glass because its adhesion to glass is greater than its cohesion. In mercury cohesion is greater, so the surface is convex.

quiz.q: If all the sides of a cube are made 3 times longer, how does its strength change?
quiz.e: The cross-sectional area becomes 9 times and the volume 27 times larger. Strength depends on the ratio of cross-section to volume, so it drops to 9/27 = 1/3.
y: Strength does not grow when the side triples. The cross-sectional area grows 9 times and the volume 27 times, so their ratio shrinks.
Area and volume grow at different rates. The ratio of cross-sectional area to volume is inversely proportional to the side length.
You shrank the ratio by the square of the side. The area becomes 9 times and the volume 27 times larger, and 9/27 = 1/3.

basinc.title: Pressure
basinc.summary: Learn about pressure in solids, liquids, and gases, Pascal's principle, and atmospheric pressure.

olay.h: Two hemispheres that horses could not pull apart
olay.p: Otto von Guericke joined two copper hemispheres and pumped out the air inside. Teams of horses hitched to each side could not pull them apart. What was holding them together?

cards.p: Pressure is the force acting perpendicular to a unit of surface, given by P = F / A. With force in newtons and area in m², the unit is the pascal. 1 Pa = 1 N/m².
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><defs><marker id='basinc-1' viewBox='0 0 10 10' refX='9' refY='5' markerWidth='6' markerHeight='6' orient='auto-start-reverse'><path d='M0 0 L10 5 L0 10 z' fill='var(--ink)'/></marker></defs><text x='160' y='38' font-size='24' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>P = F / A</text><text x='160' y='58' font-size='11' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>pressure = perpendicular force / area</text><path d='M20 160 H300' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='1.5'/><rect x='60' y='80' width='40' height='80' fill='var(--c4)' fill-opacity='0.3' stroke='var(--c4)' stroke-width='1.5'/><rect x='180' y='125' width='100' height='35' fill='var(--c4)' fill-opacity='0.3' stroke='var(--c4)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M80 100 V140' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='2' marker-end='url(#basinc-1)'/><text x='90' y='124' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='start' font-weight='700'>W</text><path d='M230 128 V156' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='2' marker-end='url(#basinc-1)'/><text x='240' y='148' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='start' font-weight='700'>W</text><rect x='60' y='161' width='40' height='5' fill='var(--c2)'/><rect x='180' y='161' width='100' height='5' fill='var(--c1)'/><text x='80' y='186' font-size='12' fill='var(--c2)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>same W, small A</text><text x='230' y='186' font-size='12' fill='var(--c1)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>same W, large A</text></svg>
cards.key: Pressure is a scalar and has no direction. The pressure force (F = P·A) is a vector.

cards.h: Pressure of solids: it is all about area
cards.p: The edge of a knife and the tip of a thumbtack create a large pressure with a small area. Snowshoes and tank tracks spread the weight over a wide area and reduce the pressure.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><defs><marker id='basinc-2' viewBox='0 0 10 10' refX='9' refY='5' markerWidth='6' markerHeight='6' orient='auto-start-reverse'><path d='M0 0 L10 5 L0 10 z' fill='var(--ink)'/></marker></defs><rect x='14' y='110' width='292' height='60' fill='var(--c1)' fill-opacity='0.12'/><path d='M14 110 H60 M90 110 H306' stroke='var(--c1)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M60 110 V140 H90 V110' fill='none' stroke='var(--muted)' stroke-dasharray='3 3'/><rect x='60' y='72' width='30' height='68' rx='3' fill='var(--c5)' fill-opacity='0.35' stroke='var(--c5)' stroke-width='1.5'/><rect x='225' y='70' width='30' height='34' rx='3' fill='var(--c5)' fill-opacity='0.35' stroke='var(--c5)' stroke-width='1.5'/><rect x='185' y='104' width='110' height='6' rx='3' fill='var(--c3)'/><path d='M75 36 V66' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='2' marker-end='url(#basinc-2)'/><text x='83' y='56' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='start' font-weight='700'>W</text><path d='M240 36 V64' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='2' marker-end='url(#basinc-2)'/><text x='248' y='56' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='start' font-weight='700'>W</text><text x='75' y='24' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>boot</text><text x='240' y='24' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>snowshoe</text><text x='75' y='160' font-size='11' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>small area</text><text x='240' y='135' font-size='11' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>large area</text><text x='75' y='190' font-size='12' fill='var(--c2)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>sinks in: large P</text><text x='240' y='190' font-size='12' fill='var(--c3)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>stays up: small P</text></svg>
cards.key: For a uniform solid P = W/A = ρ·g·h. A solid transmits force, while an enclosed liquid transmits pressure.

cards.p: The pressure caused by the weight of a liquid is P = ρ·g·h (h is the depth, ρ the density). The shape of the container and the amount of liquid do not change it. Pressure is large at depth, which is why dams are thicker at the bottom.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><defs><marker id='basinc-3' viewBox='0 0 10 10' refX='9' refY='5' markerWidth='6' markerHeight='6' orient='auto-start-reverse'><path d='M0 0 L10 5 L0 10 z' fill='var(--ink)'/></marker></defs><rect x='31' y='50' width='99' height='120' fill='var(--c1)' fill-opacity='0.2'/><path d='M30 30 V170 H130 V30' fill='none' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='2'/><path d='M31 50 H129' stroke='var(--c1)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M50 52 V148' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='1.5' marker-start='url(#basinc-3)' marker-end='url(#basinc-3)'/><text x='58' y='104' font-size='13' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='start' font-weight='700'>h</text><path d='M130 80 Q144 80 152 100' fill='none' stroke='var(--c1)' stroke-width='2'/><path d='M130 115 Q156 115 168 145' fill='none' stroke='var(--c1)' stroke-width='2.5'/><path d='M130 150 Q170 150 186 178' fill='none' stroke='var(--c1)' stroke-width='3'/><text x='80' y='190' font-size='11' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>deep hole: stronger jet</text><path d='M215 40 V170 H300' fill='none' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M215 170 L292 62' stroke='var(--c2)' stroke-width='2.5'/><text x='207' y='46' font-size='12' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='end'>P</text><text x='300' y='188' font-size='12' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='end'>h</text><text x='258' y='26' font-size='15' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>P = ρ·g·h</text><text x='268' y='150' font-size='11' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>ρ constant</text></svg>
cards.key: In water (ρ = 1000 kg/m³) every 10 m of depth adds about 100 000 Pa.

etk.soru: Change the depth and the liquid. Water 1000, olive oil ≈ 900, mercury 13 600 kg/m³. Liquid pressure only, g = 10 m/s².

cards.p: The force on the bottom is F = P·A, and it may not equal the weight of the liquid. In a straight container F = W. In a container that widens upward F < W, and in one that narrows F > W.

cards.key: The force on a side wall comes from the average pressure: F = ρ·g·(h/2)·A.

once.soru: Two containers with equal bases hold water to the same height. One widens upward and holds more water. Which one has the larger force on its bottom?

secenekler.neden: F = P·A. The depth is the same, so the pressure is the same, and the base area is the same too. So the forces are equal. The sloping walls carry the weight of the extra water in the wide container.
The weight of the extra water rests on the sloping walls. The force on the bottom is P·A.
The pressure and the base area are the same. So the force is the same too.

cards.p: Containers joined at the bottom are called connected vessels. When a single liquid is at rest, its surface is at the same level in every arm. Teapots and water towers work on this principle.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><path d='M10 70 H310' stroke='var(--acc)' stroke-dasharray='4 3'/><path d='M30 170 H290 V145 H285 V70 H265 V145 H205 L232.6 70 H212.6 L185 145 H145 V70 H95 V145 H60 V70 H40 V145 H30 Z' fill='var(--c1)' fill-opacity='0.25'/><path d='M285 40 V145 H290 V170 H30 V145 H40 V40 M60 40 V145 H95 V40 M145 40 V145 H185 L223.7 40 M243.7 40 L205 145 H265 V40' fill='none' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='2' stroke-linejoin='round'/><text x='160' y='192' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>one liquid → same level in every arm</text><text x='160' y='26' font-size='11' fill='var(--acc)' text-anchor='middle'>same horizontal level</text></svg>
cards.key: If a U-tube holds two liquids that do not mix, then above their common level h₁·ρ₁ = h₂·ρ₂.

once.soru: You pour water into a U-shaped tube. One arm is thin and the other is wide. Where do the surfaces settle when the water is at rest?

secenekler.neden: The pressure must be equal at points of the same depth. So the surfaces are on the same horizontal line. The width of the arm makes no difference.
The thin arm holds less water, but pressure depends only on depth.
The wide arm holds more water, but pressure depends only on depth.

cards.p: Pressure applied to an enclosed liquid is transmitted unchanged to every point. This is Pascal's principle. In a hydraulic system F₁ / A₁ = F₂ / A₂. So the force is multiplied by the same factor as the area.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><defs><marker id='basinc-6' viewBox='0 0 10 10' refX='9' refY='5' markerWidth='6' markerHeight='6' orient='auto-start-reverse'><path d='M0 0 L10 5 L0 10 z' fill='var(--ink)'/></marker></defs><path d='M41 90 H79 V150 H169 V110 H289 V175 H41 Z' fill='var(--c1)' fill-opacity='0.25'/><path d='M40 70 V176 H290 V90 M170 90 V150 H80 V70' fill='none' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='2'/><rect x='41' y='82' width='38' height='8' fill='var(--muted)'/><rect x='171' y='102' width='118' height='8' fill='var(--muted)'/><rect x='205' y='68' width='50' height='34' rx='4' fill='var(--c4)' fill-opacity='0.35' stroke='var(--c4)' stroke-width='1.5'/><text x='230' y='90' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>load</text><path d='M60 36 V78' stroke='var(--c2)' stroke-width='2.5' marker-end='url(#basinc-6)'/><text x='70' y='56' font-size='13' fill='var(--c2)' text-anchor='start' font-weight='700'>F₁</text><path d='M180 98 V66' stroke='var(--c3)' stroke-width='2.5' marker-end='url(#basinc-6)'/><text x='188' y='74' font-size='13' fill='var(--c3)' text-anchor='start' font-weight='700'>F₂</text><text x='230' y='34' font-size='15' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>F₁ / A₁ = F₂ / A₂</text><text x='125' y='168' font-size='10' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>pressure is transmitted unchanged everywhere</text><text x='60' y='192' font-size='12' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>A₁ small</text><text x='230' y='192' font-size='12' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>A₂ large</text></svg>
cards.key: You gain in force but lose in distance. The large piston rises less, by the ratio of the areas.

cards.p: Air has weight too. Torricelli turned a tube full of mercury upside down, and at sea level the mercury stopped at 76 cm. That is why 1 atm = 76 cmHg ≈ 101 325 Pa.

cards.key: If you used water instead of mercury, the column would be about 10.3 m tall.

once.soru: You put a card over a glass full of water and turn the glass upside down. The water does not spill. What holds the card?

secenekler.neden: Air has weight too. The pressure of the air on the card from below is much larger than the pressure of the water in the glass.
Adhesion alone cannot hold the card. The air pressure does the real work.
A light card would fall by itself too. So something must be pushing it from below.

cards.p: As you go higher, atmospheric pressure drops, and water boils at a lower temperature. On Everest water boils at about 70 °C. A pressure cooker raises the pressure, and water boils above 100 °C.

cards.key: Boiling starts when the vapor pressure of the liquid (the pressure of its vapor) equals the outside pressure.

cards.p: Gas particles move all the time and hit the walls. These collisions create gas pressure, and the pressure is the same everywhere in the container. At constant volume, the pressure rises if the number of particles or the temperature increases.

once.soru: You heat a gas in a closed container. The volume does not change. What happens to the pressure of the gas?

secenekler.neden: Heated particles speed up and hit the walls harder and more often. So the pressure increases.
The particles do not slow down, they speed up. So the collisions get stronger.
The number of particles is the same, but their speeds increased, so the collisions get stronger.

cards.p: The pressure at a point is the sum of all the pressures above it. In an open container P = P₀ + ρ·g·h. If there is gas above the liquid, you write the gas pressure in place of P₀.

once.soru: You are 10 m deep in an open pool. The pressure of the air above is ≈ 100 000 Pa, and the pressure of 10 m of water is 100 000 Pa. What is the total pressure?

secenekler.neden: Pressures add up. The air gives 100 000 Pa and the water 100 000 Pa, for a total of 200 000 Pa, about 2 atm.
That is only the pressure of the water. You must add the pressure of the air above the water too.
Pressures add up; you do not take their average.

cards.p: A fluid speeds up where its path narrows. By Bernoulli's principle, the pressure of a fluid drops where it speeds up. In a storm, fast wind over a roof lowers the pressure, and the air inside can push the roof off.

cards.key: When a fast train passes, stand behind the line on the platform. The fast air next to the train lowers the pressure.

once.soru: You hold two sheets of paper face to face and blow between them. What do the sheets do?

secenekler.neden: The pressure of the air speeding up between the sheets drops. The pressure of the still air outside pushes the sheets inward.
Intuition says so, but the pressure of air drops when it speeds up.
The pressure drops in between, so the sheets move.

cards.p:
• Pressure is P = F / A, and its unit is the pascal.
• For a solid, a smaller area means a larger pressure.
• Liquid pressure is P = ρ·g·h, and it does not depend on the shape of the container.
• By Pascal's principle F₁ / A₁ = F₂ / A₂.
• 1 atm = 76 cmHg ≈ 101 325 Pa, and it drops as you go higher.

quiz.q: In a hydraulic lift the small piston has an area of 10 cm² and the large one 200 cm². If you apply 50 N to the small piston, what is the largest load, in N, that the large piston can balance?
quiz.e: Since F₁ / A₁ = F₂ / A₂, F₂ = 50 · 200 / 10 = 1000 N. The area is 20 times larger, so the force is 20 times larger too.

quiz.q: Put the liquid pressures at the given points in open containers in order from smallest to largest.
ogeler: 25 cm deep in salt water (ρ = 1.2 g/cm³)
quiz.e: P = ρ·g·h, and g is the same for all. So look at the products h·ρ: 20·1 = 20, 30·0.8 = 24, 25·1.2 = 30, and 10·13.6 = 136. Even at a small depth, mercury gives the largest pressure.

quiz.q: Three containers with equal base areas are filled with water to the same height. Match each container with the relation between the liquid force F on its bottom and the weight W of the water.
quiz.e: In all three F = ρ·g·h·A is the same. The widening container holds more water, so W is larger and F < W; the narrowing container holds less water, so F > W.

quiz.q: In an open-end manometer connected to a gas tank, the water in the open arm stands 30 cm higher than on the gas side. If atmospheric pressure is 100 000 Pa and g = 10 m/s², what is the pressure of the gas, in Pa?
quiz.e: If the water is higher in the open arm, the gas pressure exceeds atmospheric pressure by ρ·g·h. So P = 100 000 + 1000·10·0.3 = 103 000 Pa.

kaldirma-kuvveti.title: Buoyancy
kaldirma-kuvveti.summary: Archimedes' principle, floating and sinking, ships, hydrometers, and balloons.

cards.h: Where does the buoyant force come from?
cards.p: The bottom face of a submerged object is deeper. So the push from below is larger than the push from above. The forces on the sides cancel. The difference is the upward buoyant force (Fb).

cards.p: By Archimedes' principle, the buoyant force equals the weight of the liquid the object displaces. It is given by Fb = Vsub·ρliq·g (g ≈ 10 m/s²).

once.soru: An object with 200 cm³ under water displaces 200 cm³ of water. This water weighs 2 N. What is the buoyant force on the object, in N?

secenekler.neden: The buoyant force equals the weight of the displaced liquid. This is Archimedes' principle.
A liquid exerts a buoyant force on every object submerged in it.
200 cm³ of water is 0.2 kg, and it weighs 2 N.

cards.h: Weighing in air and in a liquid
cards.p: In air a spring scale shows the weight of the object (W). In water the reading drops, because the buoyant force pushes the object up. This new reading is called the apparent weight, and it equals W − Fb.

cards.h: What changes as you go deeper?
cards.p: When a fully submerged object goes deeper, the pressures on its top and bottom faces increase by the same amount. The difference, F<sub>b</sub>, stays constant. If a partly submerged object is pushed down, F<sub>b</sub> increases.

once.soru: Wood with a density of 0.6 g/cm³ and iron with 7.8 g/cm³ are put in water (1 g/cm³). Which one floats?

secenekler.neden: What is less dense than water floats, and what is denser sinks. With equal densities it would stay suspended.
Iron is about 8 times denser than water, so it sinks.
Iron is denser than water, so it cannot float.

cards.h: How deep does a floating object sit?
cards.p: For a floating object, Fb = W gives Vsub / V = ρobj / ρliq. The density of ice is about 0.9 g/cm³. So nine tenths of the ice stays under water.

etk.soru: Change the density of the object and of the liquid. How much of the object is submerged?
yorum: The object floats. F<sub>b</sub> = W, and part of the object stays out of the liquid.
The object stays suspended. It is fully submerged, and F<sub>b</sub> = W.
The object sinks. F<sub>b</sub> < W, and the object rests on the bottom.

cards.p: For a submerged cork tied to the bottom by a string, Fb = W + T. For a stone hanging from a string and lowered into water, T + Fb = W. Here T is the apparent weight.

once.soru: A cork tied to the bottom by a string is fully under water. The string is taut. What happens if you cut the string?

secenekler.neden: The buoyant force is larger than the weight. The string was holding the difference, so F<sub>b</sub> = W + T.
The string is taut, so it was pulling the cork down.
Cork is less dense than water. So it rises when the string is cut.

cards.h: At the boundary of two liquids
cards.p: An object at the boundary of two liquids that do not mix gets a buoyant force from both. It is given by Fb = V₁·ρ₁·g + V₂·ρ₂·g. At equilibrium Fb = W.

once.soru: A cube rests in equilibrium half in water (1 g/cm³) and half in the oil above (0.8 g/cm³). What is the density of the cube?

secenekler.neden: The object gets a buoyant force from both liquids. If it sits half in each, its density is the average of the two: (1 + 0.8) / 2 = 0.9.
Then it would stay suspended entirely in the water.
Then it would stay suspended in the oil.

cards.p: Steel sinks, but a ship floats. The reason is that a ship is a shell full of air, and its average density is lower than water's. A loaded ship sits deeper.

cards.p: A hydrometer is a glass float with a heavy bottom, and in every liquid Fb = W. It sinks less in a dense liquid and more in a thin one. The density is read from the mark on its stem.

cards.key: The scale increases downward. In a dense liquid the surface meets the lower marks on the stem.

once.soru: You put a glass rod that floats in any liquid first in salt water, then in fresh water. In which one does it sink deeper?

secenekler.neden: For a floating object F<sub>b</sub> = W is constant. Fresh water is less dense, so the object must sink deeper to get the same buoyant force.
Salt water is denser. The same force is reached with less sinking.
The liquids have different densities, so the submerged volume is different too.

cards.p: Air is a fluid too, and it exerts a buoyant force on objects in it. Helium (about 0.17 kg/m³) is less dense than air (about 1.2 kg/m³). That is why a balloon rises. Hot air also becomes less dense and rises.

cards.key: 1 m³ of helium gets a buoyant force of about 12 N, and its own weight is about 1.7 N. The net lift is about 10 N.

cards.h: The overflow can and the scale
cards.p: A full overflow can spills as much liquid as the submerged volume of the object. The weight of the spilled liquid equals Fb. In a container that does not overflow, an object raises the scale reading by W. If the object hangs from a string, the increase is Fb.

once.soru: You drop a stone into an overflow can filled to the brim, and the stone sinks. What does the weight of the spilled water equal?

secenekler.neden: The spilled water equals the submerged volume of the stone. By Archimedes' principle the weight of this water equals the buoyant force.
The stone sank, so its weight is larger than the buoyant force. The spilled water is lighter than the stone.
The weight of the can does not change. The spilled water depends only on the submerged volume of the stone.

cards.p:
• The buoyant force is Fb = Vsub·ρliq·g, and it comes from a pressure difference.
• The apparent weight is W − Fb.
• For floating and suspended objects Fb = W.
• For a fully submerged object, depth does not change Fb.
• Gases exert a buoyant force too.

quiz.q: A stone reads 12 N on a spring scale in air and 8 N when fully submerged in water. If the density of water is 1 g/cm³ and g = 10 m/s², what is the density of the stone, in g/cm³?
quiz.e: Since F<sub>b</sub> = 12 − 8 = 4 N, V = 400 cm³. The mass is 1.2 kg, or 1200 g, so ρ = 1200 / 400 = 3 g/cm³.

quiz.q: The objects are put in water (ρ = 1 g/cm³). Choose what each one does.
quiz.e: An object less dense than water floats partly submerged. An object that sits half submerged is floating too. An object with the same density as water stays suspended. An object denser than water sinks, and for it F<sub>b</sub> < W.

quiz.q: A cork with a volume of 200 cm³ and a density of 0.6 g/cm³ is tied to the bottom of a container by a string and is fully under water. If g = 10 m/s², what is the tension in the string, in N?
quiz.e: F<sub>b</sub> = 0.0002 · 1000 · 10 = 2 N and W = 0.12 kg · 10 = 1.2 N. The cork is in equilibrium, so F<sub>b</sub> = W + T. That gives T = 2 − 1.2 = 0.8 N.

quiz.q: The same object floats in liquid X with half its volume submerged, stays suspended in liquid Y, and sinks to the bottom in liquid Z. Which is true for the buoyant forces on the object?
quiz.e: For floating and suspended objects F<sub>b</sub> = W. In liquid Z, where the object sinks, F<sub>b</sub> < W.
y: For floating and suspended objects the buoyant force equals the weight, so F<sub>X</sub> and F<sub>Y</sub> must be equal.
How deep an object sits does not set the force by itself. For an object that sinks, the buoyant force is smaller than the weight.
For an object that sinks to the bottom, the buoyant force is smaller than the weight. Otherwise it would not sink.

isi-sicaklik.title: Heat, temperature and expansion
isi-sicaklik.summary: Learn about temperature, heat, specific heat, changes of state, heat transfer and expansion.

cards.p: Temperature is a measure of the average kinetic energy of the particles. As tea heats up, its particles move faster. Temperature does not depend on the amount of matter. A boiling drop and a boiling bucket of water are both at 100 °C.

cards.p: Heat is energy transferred from hot to cold because of a temperature difference, so an object does not contain heat. Internal energy is the total energy of the particles, and it depends on the amount. The unit of heat is the joule (J) or the calorie.
