cards.key: Heat flows from higher temperature to lower temperature, not from larger internal energy to smaller.

once.soru: You put a cold spoon into hot tea. Which way does heat flow?

secenekler.yazi: From the tea to the spoon
secenekler.neden: Heat is energy transferred from hot to cold because of a temperature difference.

secenekler.yazi: From the spoon to the tea
secenekler.neden: A cold spoon does not heat the tea. Heat always flows from hot to cold.
Heat flows as long as the temperatures are different.

cards.p: A thermometer uses the fact that a liquid expands when it heats up. At 1 atm, water freezes at 0 °C and boils at 100 °C. Kelvin and Fahrenheit values come from T = t + 273 and F = 1.8·t + 32.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><path d='M70 50 H300 M70 150 H300' stroke='var(--line)' stroke-dasharray='4 3'/><text x='10' y='54' font-size='11' fill='var(--c2)' text-anchor='start' font-weight='700'>water boils</text><text x='10' y='154' font-size='11' fill='var(--c1)' text-anchor='start' font-weight='700'>water freezes</text><text x='10' y='70' font-size='10' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='start'>(1 atm)</text><rect x='105' y='36' width='10' height='122' rx='5' fill='var(--panel)' stroke='var(--ink)'/><circle cx='110' cy='162' r='8' fill='var(--c2)'/><rect x='108' y='100' width='4' height='58' fill='var(--c2)'/><text x='110' y='26' font-size='14' fill='var(--acc)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>°C</text><text x='119' y='46' font-size='11' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='start'>100</text><text x='119' y='146' font-size='11' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='start'>0</text><rect x='185' y='36' width='10' height='122' rx='5' fill='var(--panel)' stroke='var(--ink)'/><circle cx='190' cy='162' r='8' fill='var(--c2)'/><rect x='188' y='100' width='4' height='58' fill='var(--c2)'/><text x='190' y='26' font-size='14' fill='var(--acc)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>°F</text><text x='199' y='46' font-size='11' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='start'>212</text><text x='199' y='146' font-size='11' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='start'>32</text><rect x='265' y='36' width='10' height='122' rx='5' fill='var(--panel)' stroke='var(--ink)'/><circle cx='270' cy='162' r='8' fill='var(--c2)'/><rect x='268' y='100' width='4' height='58' fill='var(--c2)'/><text x='270' y='26' font-size='14' fill='var(--acc)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>K</text><text x='279' y='46' font-size='11' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='start'>373</text><text x='279' y='146' font-size='11' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='start'>273</text><text x='160' y='192' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>C / 100 = (F − 32) / 180 = (T − 273) / 100</text></svg>
cards.key: As a temperature difference, 1 °C = 1 K = 1.8 °F. The Kelvin scale has no negative values, and 0 K is about −273 °C.

cards.p: This difference is called specific heat (c). Specific heat is the heat that raises the temperature of 1 g of a substance by 1 °C. The specific heat of water is 1 cal/g·°C, larger than that of most substances. The heat absorbed is Q = m·c·ΔT.

cards.key: Specific heat identifies a substance. Heat capacity depends on mass, so it does not identify one.

cards.p: When objects at different temperatures touch, heat flows until the temperatures are equal. This is called thermal equilibrium. If no heat is lost to the surroundings, heat gained equals heat lost.

cards.key: The equilibrium temperature lies between the two starting temperatures. For the same substance, it is closer to the temperature of the larger mass.

etk.soru: Mix hot water with water at 20 °C. No heat is lost. Both are water, so c is the same.

ciktilar.ad: Heat gained by the cold water

cards.h: Changes of state and latent heat
cards.p: When a pure substance changes state at constant pressure, the heat it absorbs goes into overcoming the attraction between particles, and the temperature does not change. The heat needed is Q = m·L (L: heat of fusion or vaporization).

cards.p: The temperature-time graph of ice heated at constant power looks like steps. On the sloped parts the temperature rises (Q = m·c·ΔT). On the flat parts the state changes (Q = m·L).
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><path d='M50 20 V170 H300' fill='none' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M50 140 H60 M50 70 H200' stroke='var(--line)' stroke-dasharray='3 3'/><path d='M50 154 L60 140 H100 L200 70 H280 L292 50' fill='none' stroke='var(--acc)' stroke-width='2.5'/><path d='M60 140 H100 M200 70 H280' stroke='var(--c2)' stroke-width='4'/><text x='44' y='144' font-size='11' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='end'>0</text><text x='44' y='74' font-size='11' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='end'>100</text><text x='80' y='130' font-size='11' fill='var(--c2)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>melting</text><text x='240' y='60' font-size='11' fill='var(--c2)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>boiling</text><text x='62' y='162' font-size='10' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='start'>ice</text><text x='160' y='126' font-size='10' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='start'>water warms</text><text x='300' y='38' font-size='10' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='end'>steam</text><text x='58' y='24' font-size='11' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='start'>T (°C)</text><text x='52' y='188' font-size='10' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='start'>constant heating power, 1 atm</text><text x='300' y='188' font-size='11' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='end'>time</text></svg>
cards.key: On a flat part, heat is absorbed and internal energy rises, but the temperature stays constant.

etk.soru: What happens on each part of the heating curve?

noktalar.acik: On this sloped part, Q = m·c<sub>ice</sub>·ΔT. The specific heat of ice is small, so this line is steep.
On the flat part at 0 °C, the heat absorbed (Q = m·L<sub>fusion</sub>) overcomes the attraction between particles, and the temperature does not change.
On this part, Q = m·c<sub>water</sub>·ΔT. The specific heat of water is large, so the line is less steep.
On the flat part at 100 °C, Q = m·L<sub>vaporization</sub>. The heat of vaporization is larger than the heat of fusion, so this flat part is longer.
Once all the water has turned into steam, the temperature rises again.

once.soru: You heat ice at constant power. What does the temperature-time graph look like while the ice melts?

secenekler.neden: While it melts, the heat absorbed goes into the change of state. The temperature stays constant and the graph goes flat.
The temperature does not rise until the melting is over.
The temperature of ice that absorbs heat does not fall.

cards.h: Is any ice left in the mixture?
cards.p: Is any ice left? Compare the heats. If the heat the water can give off while cooling to 0 °C is not enough to melt all the ice, the equilibrium is at 0 °C and some ice remains.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><text x='160' y='22' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='bold'>100 g of ice at 0 °C + 200 g of water at 20 °C</text><text x='20' y='56' font-size='11' fill='var(--muted)'>water can give off, cooling 20 → 0 °C</text><rect x='20' y='63' width='140' height='22' rx='4' fill='var(--c2)' fill-opacity='0.35' stroke='var(--c2)'/><text x='168' y='79' font-size='12' fill='var(--c2)' font-weight='bold'>200·1·20 = 4000 cal</text><text x='20' y='110' font-size='11' fill='var(--muted)'>needed to melt all the ice</text><rect x='20' y='117' width='280' height='22' rx='4' fill='var(--c1)' fill-opacity='0.35' stroke='var(--c1)'/><text x='160' y='133' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='bold'>100·80 = 8000 cal</text><text x='160' y='168' font-size='12' fill='var(--c3)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='bold'>4000 < 8000 → 4000 / 80 = 50 g of ice melts</text><text x='160' y='188' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>equilibrium at 0 °C; 50 g of ice left</text></svg>

once.soru: You drop 100 g of ice at 0 °C into 200 g of water at 20 °C. The water gives off 4000 cal while cooling to 0 °C. Melting all the ice takes 8000 cal. What happens in the end?

secenekler.neden: 4000 cal melts only 50 g of ice (L = 80 cal/g). The equilibrium is at 0 °C and 50 g of ice remains.
That would take 8000 cal. The water can give off 4000 cal at most.
To freeze, the water must give off heat, but the ice is at 0 °C and cannot absorb that heat.

cards.p: Evaporation happens at any temperature, at the surface. The fast particles escape, so the liquid cools. Boiling happens at a specific temperature, with bubbles throughout the liquid. When the outside pressure drops, the boiling point drops too.

cards.key: Impurities lower the freezing point and raise the boiling point. That is why salt is spread on roads in winter.

once.soru: After sweating, you feel cold in the wind. Why?

secenekler.neden: During evaporation the fastest particles escape. The sweat left behind and your skin cool down.
Wet skin feels cold in a warm wind too. The real cause is evaporation.
Sweat is at body temperature. What cools you is its evaporation.

cards.p: In conduction, heat passes from particle to particle, and metals conduct well. In convection, a heated fluid rises and carries the heat. In radiation, heat travels as waves, even through empty space. Air and wool insulate.

once.soru: In the same room, a metal door handle feels colder than a wooden table. Why?

secenekler.neden: Both are at room temperature. Metal draws heat from your hand quickly, so it feels cold.

secenekler.yazi: The metal is at a lower temperature
secenekler.neden: In the same room both are at the same temperature. The difference is in conduction.
Wood does not produce heat. It just conducts heat slowly.

cards.h: What does the rate of conduction depend on?
cards.p: The heat conducted increases with a larger temperature difference and cross-sectional area, and decreases with greater thickness. The material matters too. For example, copper conducts heat much better than glass.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><text x='160' y='26' font-size='14' fill='var(--c3)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='bold'>Q / t = k·A·(T₁ − T₂) / L</text><rect x='20' y='60' width='50' height='90' rx='4' fill='var(--c2)' fill-opacity='0.35' stroke='var(--c2)'/><text x='45' y='110' font-size='13' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='bold'>T₁</text><text x='45' y='168' font-size='11' fill='var(--c2)' text-anchor='middle'>hot</text><rect x='250' y='60' width='50' height='90' rx='4' fill='var(--c1)' fill-opacity='0.35' stroke='var(--c1)'/><text x='275' y='110' font-size='13' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='bold'>T₂</text><text x='275' y='168' font-size='11' fill='var(--c1)' text-anchor='middle'>cold</text><rect x='70' y='90' width='180' height='30' fill='var(--c4)' fill-opacity='0.3' stroke='var(--c4)' stroke-width='1.5'/><line x1='95' y1='105' x2='218' y2='105' stroke='var(--c2)' stroke-width='2' fill='none'/><polygon points='225,105 215,109.5 215,100.5' fill='var(--c2)'/><text x='160' y='84' font-size='11' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>cross-sectional area A</text><line x1='76' y1='136' x2='244' y2='136' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='1.5' fill='none'/><polygon points='250,136 242,139.5 242,132.5' fill='var(--ink)'/><polygon points='70,136 78,139.5 78,132.5' fill='var(--ink)'/><text x='160' y='152' font-size='11' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>length (thickness) L</text><text x='160' y='190' font-size='11' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>k: thermal conductivity of the material (large for copper)</text></svg>

once.soru: If the outer wall of a house is made thicker, what happens to the heat escaping through it?

secenekler.neden: The heat has to be conducted along a longer path. As thickness increases, the heat conducted decreases.
A thick wall conducts less heat, not more.
The heat conducted depends on thickness, and a thick wall holds the heat in.

cards.p: A heated solid gets longer, and the change in length is ΔL = L₀·λ·ΔT. λ is the coefficient of linear expansion, and it identifies the material. For steel, λ is about 1.2·10−5 1/°C. An object that cools gets shorter.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><text x='160' y='34' font-size='22' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='800'>ΔL = L₀ · λ · ΔT</text><rect x='30' y='58' width='170' height='16' rx='3' fill='var(--c1)' fill-opacity='0.35' stroke='var(--c1)'/><text x='210' y='71' font-size='11' fill='var(--c1)' text-anchor='start' font-weight='700'>L₀ (cold)</text><rect x='30' y='100' width='200' height='16' rx='3' fill='var(--c2)' fill-opacity='0.35' stroke='var(--c2)'/><text x='240' y='113' font-size='11' fill='var(--c2)' text-anchor='start' font-weight='700'>heated</text><path d='M200 54 V136' stroke='var(--muted)' stroke-dasharray='3 3'/><path d='M200 130 H230 M200 125 V135 M230 125 V135 M230 120 V135' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='1.5'/><text x='215' y='150' font-size='12' fill='var(--acc)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>ΔL</text><text x='160' y='174' font-size='11' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>steel rail: L₀ = 10 m, ΔT = 40 °C → ΔL ≈ 4.8 mm</text><text x='160' y='192' font-size='10' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>λ (steel) ≈ 1.2 · 10⁻⁵ 1/°C</text></svg>
cards.key: The change in length is directly proportional to the original length and to the temperature change.

cards.p: A heated plate expands in every direction (ΔA ≈ A₀·2λ·ΔT), and a hole in it gets bigger too. Liquids expand more than solids, and gases expand the most.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><text x='160' y='24' font-size='13' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>area: ΔA ≈ A₀ · 2λ · ΔT</text><text x='160' y='44' font-size='13' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>volume: ΔV ≈ V₀ · 3λ · ΔT</text><path d='M150 60 V190' stroke='var(--line)'/><rect x='30' y='72' width='100' height='66' fill='var(--c4)' fill-opacity='0.35' stroke='var(--ink)'/><rect x='24' y='67' width='112' height='76' fill='none' stroke='var(--c2)' stroke-dasharray='4 3'/><circle cx='80' cy='105' r='14' fill='var(--panel)' stroke='var(--ink)'/><circle cx='80' cy='105' r='17' fill='none' stroke='var(--c2)' stroke-dasharray='3 3'/><text x='80' y='166' font-size='12' fill='var(--acc)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>the hole grows too</text><text x='80' y='186' font-size='10' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>every part of the plate expands</text><path d='M205 76 V146 H275 V76' fill='none' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='2'/><rect x='206' y='78' width='68' height='67' fill='var(--c1)' fill-opacity='0.3'/><path d='M206 78 Q240 70 274 78' fill='var(--c1)' fill-opacity='0.3' stroke='var(--c1)'/><path d='M276 76 q8 2 8 14 v20' fill='none' stroke='var(--c1)' stroke-width='2'/><circle cx='284' cy='116' r='3' fill='var(--c1)'/><text x='240' y='166' font-size='11' fill='var(--acc)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>a full container overflows</text><text x='240' y='186' font-size='10' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>liquid expands more</text></svg>
cards.key: A container filled to the brim overflows when heated, because the liquid expands more than the container.

once.soru: You heat a metal plate with a hole in the middle. What happens to the hole?

secenekler.neden: The plate expands in every direction. The edge of the hole also stretches outward, and the hole gets bigger.
Intuition says so, but every part of the plate gets longer, including the edge of the hole.
The edge of the hole is metal too, and it expands.

cards.p: As water warms from 0 °C to 4 °C it contracts, and its density is greatest at 4 °C. Surface water that cools sinks to the bottom. In the end the surface freezes, and water at 4 °C stays at the bottom.

cards.key: When water freezes, its volume increases by about 9%. That is why pipes and rocks crack in winter.

once.soru: When a lake freezes in winter, where does the ice form?

secenekler.neden: Water is densest at 4 °C, and surface water that cools sinks to the bottom. The surface reaches 0 °C last and freezes. The ice insulates, and living things survive beneath it.
Ice is less dense than water, so it cannot stay at the bottom.
Water close to 4 °C stays at the bottom. Freezing happens at the surface.

cards.p: In summer, wires sag and bridge joints narrow. A bimetallic strip is made of two metal strips with different expansion coefficients. When heated, it bends toward the metal that expands less, and it is used as a switch in thermostats and irons.

cards.key: Hold a stuck metal jar lid under hot water. Metal expands more than glass, and the lid loosens.

once.soru: A stuck metal jar lid opens easily after you hold it under hot water. Why?

secenekler.neden: The heated metal lid expands more than the glass rim and loosens.
Hot water does not melt glass.
Metal does not soften at this temperature. It just gets a little bigger.

cards.p:
• Temperature is a measure of average kinetic energy, and heat is energy that is transferred.
• T = t + 273 and F = 1.8·t + 32.
• Heat is Q = m·c·ΔT, and Q = m·L during a change of state.
• At thermal equilibrium, heat gained equals heat lost.
• The change in length is ΔL = L₀·λ·ΔT, and water is densest at 4 °C.

quiz.q: In a container with no heat loss, 100 g of water at 90 °C is mixed with 200 g of water at 30 °C. What is the equilibrium temperature in °C?
quiz.e: Heat gained equals heat lost: 100·(90 − T) = 200·(T − 30). This gives T = 50 °C. The equilibrium temperature is closer to that of the water with the larger mass.

quiz.q: Ice at −20 °C is heated at constant power at 1 atm until it turns into steam. Put the stages in order.
ogeler: Ice warms, its temperature rises to 0 °C
Ice melts, the temperature stays at 0 °C
Water warms, its temperature rises to 100 °C
Water boils, the temperature stays at 100 °C
Steam warms, its temperature rises above 100 °C
quiz.e: On the sloped parts the temperature rises (Q = m·c·ΔT), and on the flat parts the state changes (Q = m·L). In order: the ice warms, it melts, the water warms, it boils, and the steam warms.

quiz.q: Match each event with the concept that explains it.
ciftler: The handle of a pot on the stove getting hot
Warm air rising in a room
quiz.e: In the metal handle, heat is conducted from particle to particle. Heated air rises and carries heat by convection. The Sun's heat arrives through empty space by radiation. As sweat evaporates, the fastest particles escape and the skin cools. Heated wires expand and get longer.

quiz.q: A metal plate with a circular hole in the middle is heated. How does the diameter of the hole change?
quiz.e: A heated plate expands by the same ratio in every direction, like a photograph being enlarged. The hole grows just as it would if it were filled with metal.
y: The plate does not expand inward. It expands proportionally in every direction. The rim of the hole also gets longer, and the hole gets bigger.
There is no material in the hole, but the metal around it expands. The edges of the hole move away from each other.
Expansion is a steady growth from start to finish. The hole never gets smaller first. It keeps getting bigger.

basit-harmonik-hareket.title: Simple harmonic motion
basit-harmonik-hareket.summary: Learn about the restoring force, oscillation graphs, pendulums and energy.

cards.p: When you pull an object a distance x from equilibrium, a spring pulls it back with a force F = −k·x. This force always points toward equilibrium. Motion under such a force is called simple harmonic motion (SHM).

once.soru: A swing makes one full back-and-forth trip in 4 seconds. What is its frequency?

secenekler.neden: f = 1/T = 1/4 = 0.25 Hz. So the object makes a quarter of an oscillation each second.
4 is the period. Frequency is the inverse of the period.
For 2 oscillations per second the period would have to be 0.5 s.

once.soru: You follow one cabin of a Ferris wheel by its shadow on the ground. How does the shadow move?

secenekler.neden: The shadow shows only the horizontal position, and it goes back and forth between two ends.
The shadow falls on the ground and stays on a straight line.
As the cabin turns, the position of the shadow changes.

cards.p: If the object is at +A at t = 0, then x = A·cos(ωt). It passes equilibrium at T/4, reaches −A at T/2, and is back at the start at T. The slope of the graph is the velocity.
cards.key: If it starts from equilibrium in the + direction, you write x = A·sin(ωt). At the peaks and troughs the slope, and so the velocity, is zero.

cards.p: The speed is |v| = ω√(A² − x²). At equilibrium (x = 0) the speed is greatest: vmax = ωA. At the ends (x = ±A) the object stops for an instant.

once.soru: Where is an oscillating object fastest?

secenekler.neden: The force keeps speeding the object up all the way from the end to equilibrium. So the speed is greatest at equilibrium.
At the ends the object stops for an instant and turns back.
The speed changes all the time.

cards.p: From Newton's law, ma = −kx, which gives a = −ω²x (ω² = k/m). The acceleration always points toward equilibrium. It is greatest at the ends (ω²A) and zero at equilibrium.

dy='3'>max</tspan><tspan dy='-3'> = 25·0.2 = 5 m/s²</tspan></text><text x='160' y='184' font-size='11' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>x = 0.12 m: |a| = 25·0.12 = 3 m/s²</text></svg>
cards.key: At equilibrium the force is zero, but the object does not stop. Its speed is greatest right there.

once.soru: When the object stops for an instant at an end, what is its acceleration?

secenekler.neden: At the end the displacement is greatest, so the force and the acceleration are greatest too.
What is zero at the end is the velocity, not the acceleration. The object turns back right away.
Acceleration is proportional to displacement. So it is greatest at the end.

cards.h: The phase of position, velocity and acceleration
cards.p: Position, velocity and acceleration oscillate with the same period. The acceleration graph is the position graph with the opposite sign. Velocity is shifted by T/4 from position. So when x is greatest, the velocity is zero.
cards.key: When x = 0 the speed is greatest. In a graph question, look at the x graph first. a is the same graph with the opposite sign, and v is its slope.

once.soru: When the position is +A, which way does the acceleration point?

secenekler.neden: a = −ω²x. When x is positive the acceleration is negative, so it points toward equilibrium.
The acceleration always points toward equilibrium.
The acceleration is greatest at the end.

cards.h: The period of a mass on a spring
cards.p: The period of a mass on a spring is T = 2π√(m/k). A larger mass makes the period longer, and a stiffer spring makes it shorter. The period does not depend on the amplitude. It stays the same if the spring hangs vertically or is on another planet.

cards.key: The period of a mass on a spring depends neither on the amplitude nor on g.

etk.soru: Change the mass, the spring constant and the amplitude. Does the amplitude change the period?

cards.h: Springs in series and in parallel
cards.p: Parallel springs share the load: k<sub>eq</sub> = k<sub>1</sub> + k<sub>2</sub>. In series the extensions add up and the system gets softer: 1/k<sub>eq</sub> = 1/k<sub>1</sub> + 1/k<sub>2</sub>.

cards.key: Two identical springs give 2k in parallel and k/2 in series. If you cut a spring in half, each half has a constant of 2k.

once.soru: You connect two identical springs side by side (in parallel) and hang the same mass. How does the system compare with a single spring?

secenekler.neden: The load is shared by the two springs, and each stretches half as much. So the equivalent constant is 2k.
Softening happens in a series connection.
Two springs together pull with a larger force.

cards.p: A pendulum swinging through small angles does SHM, and its period is T = 2π√(L/g). The period does not depend on the mass. A longer string makes the period longer, and a larger g makes it shorter.

cards.key: The angle should be below about 10°. For L = 1 m and g = 9.8 m/s², T is about 2 s.

cards.h: In an elevator and on another planet
cards.p: For a pendulum, you use the effective acceleration g' in place of g. If the elevator accelerates upward, g' = g + a, and if it accelerates downward, g' = g − a. In free fall there is no oscillation.

cards.key: What matters is the direction of the acceleration, not of the velocity. In an elevator moving at constant speed the period does not change.

cards.p: Without friction the total energy is constant: E = ½kA². At position x the potential energy is Ep = ½kx². At the ends all the energy is potential, and at equilibrium it is all kinetic.
cards.key: At x = A/√2 the kinetic and potential energies are equal. If the amplitude doubles, the energy becomes 4 times larger.

cards.p: Friction turns the energy into heat, and the amplitude shrinks. This is called damped oscillation. If you push the system regularly at its own natural frequency, the amplitude grows very large. This is called resonance.
cards.key: For resonance, the frequency of the outside push must equal the natural frequency. Pushing a swing at the right moments is an example.

cards.p:
• The restoring force is F = −kx, and it points toward equilibrium.
• The speed is greatest at equilibrium (ωA), and the acceleration at the ends (ω²A).
• The periods are 2π√(m/k) and 2π√(L/g), and they do not depend on the amplitude.
• For parallel springs k adds up, and for series springs 1/k adds up.
• The total energy is E = ½kA².

quiz.q: An object in simple harmonic motion has an amplitude of 0.1 m and an angular frequency of 10 rad/s. What is its speed, in m/s, 0.06 m from the equilibrium point?
In a mass-spring system, where is each quantity greatest? Put each one in the right group.
quiz.e: At equilibrium x = 0. There the speed is greatest, at ωA, and all the energy is kinetic. At the ends |x| = A, so the force (kx), the acceleration (ω²A) and the potential energy (½kA²) are greatest.

quiz.q: In a mass-spring system, what does each change do to the period? Match them.
ciftler: The spring constant becomes 4 times larger
An identical second spring is added in series
quiz.e: T = 2π√(m/k). When m becomes 4 times larger, T doubles, and when k becomes 4 times larger, T is cut in half. The amplitude does not affect the period. In series k<sub>eq</sub> = k/2, so T is multiplied by √2.

quiz.q: A simple pendulum and a mass on a spring oscillate in an elevator that accelerates upward. How do their periods change compared with an elevator at rest?
o: The pendulum's gets shorter, the spring's does not change
The pendulum's gets longer, the spring's does not change
quiz.e: If the acceleration is upward, the effective gravity for the pendulum is g' = g + a, which is larger. So T = 2π√(L/g') gets shorter. For the mass on a spring, T = 2π√(m/k) does not contain g and does not change.
y: The period of a mass on a spring is T = 2π√(m/k). It does not depend on g, so it does not depend on the acceleration of the elevator.
With upward acceleration g' = g + a. When g' is larger, the period of the pendulum gets shorter, not longer.
For a simple pendulum T = 2π√(L/g'), so the period depends on the effective gravity. In an accelerating elevator g' changes.

dalgalar.title: Vibrations and waves
dalgalar.summary: Types of waves, reflection, interference, sound and electromagnetic waves.

cards.p: A vibration that travels through a medium is called a mechanical wave, and a wave carries energy. If the vibration is perpendicular to the direction of travel, the wave is transverse. A wave on a rope is an example. If the vibration is parallel to the direction of travel, the wave is longitudinal. Sound is an example.
cards.key: Light is a transverse wave too, but it is not mechanical. Light needs no medium and travels through a vacuum.

cards.p: The distance between two neighboring crests is the wavelength (λ). The height from equilibrium to a crest is the amplitude (A), and the number of waves per second is the frequency. The speed of the wave is v = λ·f.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><defs><marker id='dalga-4' viewBox='0 0 10 10' refX='9' refY='5' markerWidth='6' markerHeight='6' orient='auto-start-reverse'><path d='M0 0 L10 5 L0 10 z' fill='var(--ink)'/></marker></defs><path d='M10 110 H300' fill='none' stroke='var(--muted)' stroke-width='1' stroke-dasharray='3 3'/><path d='M20 110 Q50 30 80 110 T140 110 T200 110 T260 110' fill='none' stroke='var(--c1)' stroke-width='2.5'/><path d='M50 58 V68 M170 58 V68' fill='none' stroke='var(--muted)' stroke-width='1'/><path d='M52 58 H168' fill='none' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='1.5' marker-end='url(#dalga-4)' marker-start='url(#dalga-4)'/><text x='110' y='50' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>λ (wavelength)</text><path d='M232 150 H286' fill='none' stroke='var(--muted)' stroke-width='1' stroke-dasharray='3 3'/><path d='M278 112 V148' fill='none' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='1.5' marker-end='url(#dalga-4)' marker-start='url(#dalga-4)'/><text x='288' y='135' font-size='13' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='start' font-weight='700'>A</text><text x='110' y='170' font-size='11' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>trough</text><text x='250' y='30' font-size='18' fill='var(--c2)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>v = λ·f</text><text x='250' y='50' font-size='12' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>T = 1/f</text><text x='170' y='192' font-size='11' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>f: number of waves per second (Hz)</text></svg>
cards.key: The period is T = 1/f. The amplitude sets the energy. When the amplitude doubles, the energy becomes 4 times larger.

etk.soru: Change the wavelength and the frequency: v = λ·f.

cards.h: Speed depends on the medium, frequency on the source
cards.p: The medium sets the speed of a wave. A wave travels fast on a tight rope and slowly on a thick rope. The source sets the frequency. When a wave enters another medium, f does not change, but λ does.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><defs><marker id='dalga-5' viewBox='0 0 10 10' refX='9' refY='5' markerWidth='6' markerHeight='6' orient='auto-start-reverse'><path d='M0 0 L10 5 L0 10 z' fill='var(--ink)'/></marker></defs><text x='160' y='22' font-size='12' fill='var(--c2)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>f stays the same</text><path d='M160 34 V128' fill='none' stroke='var(--muted)' stroke-width='1' stroke-dasharray='3 3'/><path d='M0 100 Q20 60 40 100 T80 100 T120 100 T160 100' fill='none' stroke='var(--c1)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M160 100 Q170 70 180 100 T200 100 T220 100 T240 100 T260 100 T280 100 T300 100' fill='none' stroke='var(--c1)' stroke-width='4'/><path d='M22 64 H98' fill='none' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='1.2' marker-end='url(#dalga-5)' marker-start='url(#dalga-5)'/><text x='60' y='56' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>λ₁</text><path d='M172 74 H208' fill='none' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='1.2' marker-end='url(#dalga-5)' marker-start='url(#dalga-5)'/><text x='190' y='64' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>λ₂</text><text x='80' y='150' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>thin spring</text><text x='235' y='150' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>thick spring</text><text x='80' y='170' font-size='11' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>large v, long λ</text><text x='235' y='170' font-size='11' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>small v, short λ</text><text x='160' y='192' font-size='11' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>v = λ·f: with f constant, v and λ change by the same ratio</text></svg>
cards.key: On a stretched rope v = √(F/μ). F is the force stretching the rope, and μ is the mass per unit length of the rope.

cards.h: Reflection of a pulse on a spring
cards.p: A pulse reflected from a fixed end tied to a wall comes back inverted. So a crest returns as a trough. From a free end, a ring sliding on a rod, the pulse reflects upright. The transmitted pulse always stays upright.

cards.p: When two waves overlap at the same point, their displacements add. This is called interference. A crest meeting a crest gives constructive interference, and a crest meeting an equal trough gives destructive interference. The waves then continue on their way unchanged.

cards.key: In destructive interference the energy does not disappear. When the waves separate, both return to their original shape.

cards.p: Two identical waves traveling in opposite directions on the same rope form a standing wave. The points that never vibrate are nodes, and the points that vibrate with the largest amplitude are antinodes.

cards.key: The distance between two neighboring nodes or two neighboring antinodes is λ/2.

once.soru: Both ends of a guitar string are fixed. Do these ends vibrate when the string is played?

secenekler.neden: Fixed ends cannot move. So in a standing wave these ends are always nodes.
The points that vibrate most are antinodes, and they are in the middle of the string.
Tied ends do not vibrate at all.

once.soru: A water wave reaches a straight wall at 30° to the normal. What is the angle of reflection?

secenekler.neden: The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection.
60° is the angle with the wall. Angles are measured from the normal.
The angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence. 90° would not make sense here, since the wave arrives at 30°.

cards.p: Water waves slow down in a shallow region. The frequency does not change, and the wavelength gets shorter. A wave that meets the boundary at an angle is refracted. Going from deep to shallow, the wave bends toward the normal.

once.soru: Why do ocean waves turn parallel to the shore even when they approach at an angle?

secenekler.yazi: They slow down in the shallows
secenekler.neden: The part of the wave nearer the shore slows down first. So the wave front turns and becomes parallel to the shore.
Waves turn near the shore even with no wind.
The turning happens in shallow water, before the wave reaches the shore.

cards.p: A wave passing through a narrow gap bends into the region behind the barrier. This is called diffraction. Diffraction is noticeable when the gap is close to the wavelength or smaller. Two identical sources produce interference lines.

once.soru: You can hear someone behind a door but you cannot see them. Why?

secenekler.neden: The wavelength of sound is close to the size of the doorway, so sound bends around the corner. The wavelength of light is very small.
Light is much faster than sound.
Sound does not come through the wall either. It bends through the opening.

cards.p: Sound is a longitudinal, mechanical wave that compresses and thins out the air. So it does not travel through a vacuum. The speed of sound is greatest in solids and smallest in gases. In air it is about 343 m/s.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><path d='M80 42 V160' fill='none' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='1.5'/><text x='160' y='22' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>speed of sound (m/s, approximate, 20 °C)</text><text x='70' y='65' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='end' font-weight='700'>air</text><rect x='80' y='50' width='11.4' height='22' rx='3' fill='var(--c1)' fill-opacity='0.35' stroke='var(--c1)' stroke-width='1.5'/><text x='99.43333333333334' y='65' font-size='11' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='start'>343</text><text x='70' y='103' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='end' font-weight='700'>water</text><rect x='80' y='88' width='49.3' height='22' rx='3' fill='var(--c3)' fill-opacity='0.35' stroke='var(--c3)' stroke-width='1.5'/><text x='137.33333333333334' y='103' font-size='11' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='start'>≈ 1480</text><text x='70' y='141' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='end' font-weight='700'>steel</text><rect x='80' y='126' width='196.7' height='22' rx='3' fill='var(--c5)' fill-opacity='0.35' stroke='var(--c5)' stroke-width='1.5'/><text x='268.66666666666663' y='141' font-size='11' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='end'>≈ 5900</text><text x='70' y='176' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='end' font-weight='700'>vacuum</text><text x='80' y='176' font-size='12' fill='var(--c2)' text-anchor='start' font-weight='700'>0: sound does not travel</text><text x='160' y='196' font-size='11' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>in general: gas < liquid < solid</text></svg>
cards.key: Sound travels at about 1480 m/s in water. The human ear hears sounds between 20 and 20 000 Hz. Sounds below this range are called infrasound, and those above it ultrasound.

once.soru: Can we hear the sound of an explosion in space from Earth?

secenekler.neden: Sound needs matter to travel. So it cannot travel through the vacuum of space.
Sound does not travel through a vacuum at all.
We see the light, but we do not hear the sound.

cards.p: The pitch of a sound depends on its frequency. Its intensity grows with amplitude and is measured in decibels (dB). Timbre is the wave shape that lets you tell a violin from a piano.
cards.key: Every +10 dB means the intensity is 10 times larger. So a 70 dB sound has 10 times the intensity of a 60 dB sound.

once.soru: Why does the same note sound different on a violin and on a piano?

secenekler.neden: The frequency is the same, but the wave shapes are different.
The same note has the same frequency.
The air sets the speed of sound, not the source.

cards.p: You hear a higher pitch when a sound source approaches and a lower pitch when it moves away. This is called the Doppler effect. The wavelength is shorter in front of the source and longer behind it. The source's own frequency does not change.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><defs><marker id='dalga-11' viewBox='0 0 10 10' refX='9' refY='5' markerWidth='6' markerHeight='6' orient='auto-start-reverse'><path d='M0 0 L10 5 L0 10 z' fill='var(--c4)'/></marker></defs><g transform='translate(-80,0)'><text x='240' y='26' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>Doppler</text><circle cx='230' cy='100' r='60.0' fill='none' stroke='var(--c1)' stroke-width='1.5'/><circle cx='245' cy='100' r='37.5' fill='none' stroke='var(--c1)' stroke-width='1.5'/><circle cx='260' cy='100' r='15.0' fill='none' stroke='var(--c1)' stroke-width='1.5'/><circle cx='270' cy='100' r='5' fill='var(--c4)'/><path d='M276 100 H302' fill='none' stroke='var(--c4)' stroke-width='2' marker-end='url(#dalga-11)'/><text x='168' y='184' font-size='11' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='start'>behind: low</text><text x='310' y='184' font-size='11' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='end'>ahead: high</text></g></svg>
cards.key: The speed of sound in air does not change either. Speed radar and Doppler ultrasound use this effect.

once.soru: An ambulance with its siren on passes you and moves away. How does the sound change?

secenekler.neden: Behind it the wavelength is longer, so the frequency you hear drops.
The pitch rises while the source is approaching.
The source is moving, so the frequency you hear changes.

cards.p: Light, radio waves and X-rays are electromagnetic waves. They are transverse waves and need no medium. Their speed in a vacuum is c = 3×108 m/s. As the frequency increases, the wavelength gets shorter and the energy increases.
cards.key: The order is radio, microwave, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-ray and gamma. In visible light, red has the longest wavelength and violet the shortest.

etk.soru: Put the electromagnetic waves in order from shortest to longest wavelength. Hint: as the frequency increases, the wavelength gets shorter.

once.soru: How does sunlight cross empty space and reach the Earth?

secenekler.neden: An electromagnetic wave travels through a vacuum too.
Space is almost empty.
Sunlight reaches us every day.

cards.p: Ultrasound images a baby, and sonar measures depth. These are mechanical waves. Radio and phones carry communication, a microwave oven heats food, and X-rays show bones. These are electromagnetic waves.

cards.key: A mechanical wave needs a medium, while an electromagnetic wave also travels through a vacuum. A seismograph records earthquake waves, and radar finds aircraft.

once.soru: Which kind of wave carries a phone call through a satellite?

secenekler.neden: Only an electromagnetic wave can cross the vacuum of space.
Sound does not travel through a vacuum.
Ultrasound is a mechanical wave too, and it needs a medium.

cards.p:
• A wave carries energy and is transverse or longitudinal.
• v = λ·f. The speed depends on the medium, and the frequency on the source.
• A pulse reflects inverted from a fixed end and upright from a free end.
• Sound is longitudinal and does not travel through a vacuum.
• The speed of EM waves in a vacuum is c = 3×108 m/s.

quiz.q: A source produces 5 waves per second, and the distance between two neighboring crests is 0.4 m. What is the speed of the wave in m/s?
quiz.e: v = λ·f = 0.4 m · 5 Hz = 2 m/s.

quiz.q: A sound wave passes from air into water. How do its frequency, speed and wavelength change?
o: Frequency stays the same. Speed and wavelength increase
Frequency stays the same. Speed and wavelength decrease
Frequency increases. Speed and wavelength stay the same
quiz.e: The source sets the frequency, and it does not change. Sound is faster in water (about 1480 m/s) than in air (about 343 m/s). Since v = λ·f, the wavelength increases by the same ratio.
y: You assumed that what happens on a thick rope is true for sound as well. Sound is about 4 times faster in water than in air.
The source sets the frequency. When a wave enters another medium, f does not change.
The medium sets the speed. Water is a different medium, so the speed changes.

quiz.q: A pulse (a crest) travels along a spring. In each case, how does it come back or pass through? Inverted (a trough) or upright (a crest)?
ogeler: Reflected going from a thin to a thick spring
Reflected going from a thick to a thin spring
Transmitted from a thin to a thick spring
Transmitted from a thick to a thin spring
quiz.e: A fixed end and a thick spring reflect the pulse inverted. A free end and a thin spring reflect it upright. The pulse transmitted between two springs stays upright in every case.

quiz.q: When an ambulance with its siren on approaches you, you hear a higher pitch. What is the reason?
o: The frequency the siren produces increases
The speed of sound in air increases
The wave crests reach your ear closer together
The amplitude of the sound increases
quiz.e: In the Doppler effect, the source's own frequency and the speed of sound do not change. In front of an approaching source the wavelength is shorter, and you perceive a higher frequency.
y: The frequency the siren itself produces does not change. What changes is how often the waves reach your ear.
The speed of sound depends on the medium and does not change with the motion of the source. What changes is the wavelength.
Amplitude sets the intensity of the sound. A higher pitch comes from a higher frequency.

deprem.title: Earthquakes and resonance
deprem.summary: A fault breaks, waves spread out, and a building sways at its own frequency.

cards.p: Along a fault, the rocks are locked together by friction, and stress builds up for years. When the strength of the rocks is exceeded, the blocks slip suddenly. The stored energy spreads out as seismic waves.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><defs><marker id='deprem-1' viewBox='0 0 10 10' refX='9' refY='5' markerWidth='6' markerHeight='6' orient='auto'><path d='M0 0L10 5L0 10z' fill='var(--c1)'/></marker></defs><rect x='20' y='40' width='140' height='110' fill='var(--c4)' fill-opacity='0.14'/><rect x='160' y='40' width='140' height='110' fill='var(--c4)' fill-opacity='0.24'/><line x1='160' y1='34' x2='160' y2='156' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='2.5' stroke-dasharray='7 5'/><path d='M20 95 L120 95 Q160 95 160 112' fill='none' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='6' stroke-linecap='round' opacity='0.85'/><path d='M160 78 Q160 95 200 95 L300 95' fill='none' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='6' stroke-linecap='round' opacity='0.85'/><line x1='60' y1='130' x2='60' y2='106' stroke='var(--c1)' stroke-width='2' marker-end='url(#deprem-1)'/><line x1='260' y1='60' x2='260' y2='84' stroke='var(--c1)' stroke-width='2' marker-end='url(#deprem-1)'/><text x='160' y='24' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>Stress builds up on a locked fault</text><text x='168' y='150' font-size='11' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='start'>fault</text><rect x='20' y='164' width='280' height='30' rx='6' fill='var(--panel)'/><text x='160' y='184' font-size='11.5' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>past its strength the rock slips suddenly: earthquake</text></svg>
cards.key: The Earth's crust is made of plates, and the plates move a few cm each year. An earthquake is slowly built-up stress released within seconds.

cards.p: The underground point where the break starts is the focus, and the point on the surface directly above it is the epicenter. In most destructive earthquakes the focus is shallow, less than 70 km deep.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><defs><marker id='deprem-2' viewBox='0 0 10 10' refX='9' refY='5' markerWidth='6' markerHeight='6' orient='auto'><path d='M0 0L10 5L0 10z' fill='var(--muted)'/></marker></defs><rect x='10' y='60' width='300' height='130' fill='var(--c4)' fill-opacity='0.14'/><line x1='10' y1='60' x2='310' y2='60' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='2'/><circle cx='160' cy='150' r='22' fill='none' stroke='var(--c2)' stroke-width='1.5' opacity='0.9'/><circle cx='160' cy='150' r='44' fill='none' stroke='var(--c2)' stroke-width='1.5' opacity='0.6'/><circle cx='160' cy='150' r='66' fill='none' stroke='var(--c2)' stroke-width='1.5' opacity='0.35'/><circle cx='160' cy='150' r='6' fill='var(--c2)'/><line x1='160' y1='144' x2='160' y2='64' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-dasharray='4 3'/><circle cx='160' cy='60' r='5' fill='var(--ink)'/><text x='160' y='48' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>epicenter</text><text x='236' y='146' font-size='12' fill='var(--c2)' text-anchor='start' font-weight='700'>focus</text><text x='236' y='161' font-size='11' fill='var(--c2)' text-anchor='start'>(hypocenter)</text><line x1='232' y1='150' x2='168' y2='150' stroke='var(--c2)' stroke-width='1'/><text x='150' y='108' font-size='10.5' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='end'>focal depth</text><text x='160' y='22' font-size='12' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>Where the break starts, and the point above it</text></svg>
cards.key: In a shallow earthquake the energy reaches the surface with less loss. The location given in the news is the epicenter.

once.soru: The news says "the earthquake was 10 km deep." What is 10 km deep?

secenekler.yazi: The point where the break started
secenekler.neden: This point is called the focus. The depth is the distance from the surface to the focus.
Building foundations are only a few meters deep.
The depth describes the point where the break started.

cards.h: Why do earthquakes happen in certain places?
cards.p: The Earth's crust is made of slowly moving plates. At their boundaries the plates grind past each other, collide or move apart. Stress builds up on the faults at these boundaries, and most earthquakes happen there.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><text x='160' y='22' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>Plates grind past each other at a boundary</text><path d='M30 44 L176 44 L136 168 L30 168 Z' fill='var(--panel)' stroke='var(--line-2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M184 44 L290 44 L290 168 L144 168 Z' fill='var(--panel)' stroke='var(--line-2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><path d='M180 44 L140 168' fill='none' stroke='var(--c2)' stroke-width='3.5'/><path d='M96 140 L96 76 M88 88 L96 74 L104 88' fill='none' stroke='var(--c1)' stroke-width='3' stroke-linecap='round' stroke-linejoin='round'/><path d='M224 72 L224 136 M216 124 L224 138 L232 124' fill='none' stroke='var(--c1)' stroke-width='3' stroke-linecap='round' stroke-linejoin='round'/><text x='70' y='112' font-size='11.5' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>plate</text><text x='256' y='108' font-size='11.5' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>plate</text><text x='172' y='108' font-size='11.5' fill='var(--c2)' text-anchor='start' font-weight='700'>fault</text><text x='160' y='190' font-size='10.5' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>schematic; stress builds up along the fault</text></svg>
cards.key: About 90% of the world's earthquakes happen in the Ring of Fire around the Pacific. A fault map shows where an earthquake will happen, but it cannot tell when.

once.soru: Why are earthquakes frequent in Japan and Chile?

secenekler.yazi: They are on a plate boundary
secenekler.neden: Both countries sit on boundaries where plates push against each other. Stress builds up on the faults there.
Cave collapses cause very small tremors. Large earthquakes happen on faults.
Most large earthquakes come from faults, not volcanoes. Volcanoes form at the same plate boundaries.

cards.p: The P wave is longitudinal, arrives first at ≈6 km/s, and passes through every medium. The S wave is transverse, arrives later at ≈3.5 km/s, and cannot pass through liquids.

cards.key: The fact that S waves cannot pass through the outer core showed that the outer core is liquid.

cards.p: When body waves reach the surface, surface waves form. They are the slowest waves, but their amplitudes are large. Most of the damage to buildings comes from surface waves.
cards.key: The waves arrive in this order: first P, then S, and last the surface waves.

once.soru: In an earthquake there is a slight tremor first, then strong shaking. Which waves cause most of the strong shaking?

secenekler.neden: Surface waves arrive last, but their amplitudes are the largest. They shake the ground both sideways and up and down.
The P wave arrives first. It is the first slight tremor.
S is stronger than P, but surface waves have a larger amplitude.

cards.p: The S wave falls behind the P wave. The time between them (Δt) grows with distance, and each second is about 8 km. Circles drawn by three stations cross at the epicenter.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><circle cx='110' cy='80' r='58' fill='var(--c1)' fill-opacity='0.06' stroke='var(--c1)' stroke-width='1.6'/><path d='M104 85 L110 74 L116 85 Z' fill='var(--c1)'/><circle cx='230' cy='95' r='72' fill='var(--c3)' fill-opacity='0.06' stroke='var(--c3)' stroke-width='1.6'/><path d='M224 100 L230 89 L236 100 Z' fill='var(--c3)'/><circle cx='175' cy='150' r='43' fill='var(--c5)' fill-opacity='0.06' stroke='var(--c5)' stroke-width='1.6'/><path d='M169 155 L175 144 L181 155 Z' fill='var(--c5)'/><line x1='222' y1='180' x2='165' y2='114' stroke='var(--c2)' stroke-width='1.2'/><circle cx='160' cy='110' r='6' fill='var(--c2)'/><text x='226' y='188' font-size='11.5' fill='var(--c2)' text-anchor='start' font-weight='700'>epicenter</text><rect x='6' y='168' width='120' height='26' rx='6' fill='var(--panel)'/><text x='66' y='186' font-size='12.5' fill='var(--acc)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>d ≈ 8 km × Δt</text></svg>

etk.soru: Change the speeds of P and S and the time between them. How does the distance change?

cards.key: If Δt = 10 s, the earthquake is about 80 km away. One station gives only the distance.

cards.p: Magnitude is a measure of the energy released. When the magnitude goes up by 1, the energy goes up about 32 times. Intensity describes the shaking and damage at one place. It is measured from I to XII and depends on distance and on the ground.

cards.p: A seismograph relies on inertia. A heavy mass hanging from a spring tends to stay where it is, while the frame shakes with the ground. The record of the difference between them is called a seismogram.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><rect x='40' y='140' width='240' height='14' fill='var(--c4)' fill-opacity='0.5'/><line x1='80' y1='140' x2='80' y2='40' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='3'/><line x1='80' y1='40' x2='190' y2='40' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='3'/><path d='M180 40 L180 52 l-6 4 l12 6 l-12 6 l12 6 l-6 4 L180 86' fill='none' stroke='var(--muted)' stroke-width='2'/><rect x='166' y='86' width='28' height='24' rx='3' fill='var(--c1)'/><line x1='194' y1='100' x2='228' y2='100' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='1.5'/><rect x='228' y='70' width='50' height='66' fill='var(--panel)' stroke='var(--line-2)'/><path d='M232 100 L238 100 L241 92 L244 108 L247 88 L250 112 L253 96 L256 104 L260 100 L274 100' fill='none' stroke='var(--c2)' stroke-width='1.4'/><text x='150' y='22' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>Inertia holds the mass still while the frame shakes</text><text x='150' y='124' font-size='11' fill='var(--c1)' text-anchor='end' font-weight='700'>mass</text><text x='253' y='64' font-size='11' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>record</text><text x='160' y='178' font-size='11' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>the difference is recorded; today's devices are electronic</text></svg>
cards.key: With a large mass and a soft spring the device is more sensitive. Thousands of stations around the world monitor the ground all the time.

once.soru: When a bus starts suddenly, a standing passenger is thrown backward. A seismograph uses the same principle. Which one?

secenekler.neden: The heavy mass tends to stay where it is. The difference between it and the frame, which shakes with the ground, is recorded.
What a seismograph relies on is the tendency of the mass to stay at rest.
Buoyancy acts in liquids and gases. A seismograph relies on inertia.

cards.p: Every building has a natural period, roughly the number of floors times 0.1 s. If the period of the ground shaking comes close to it, the swaying grows. This is called resonance.
cards.key: The period of a 10-story building is about 1 s. In resonance, small but well-timed pushes build up a large oscillation. The same thing happens on a swing.

cards.p: On loose, wet ground the amplitude of the shaking grows and its period gets longer. This is called site amplification. The ground can also behave like a liquid, which is called liquefaction. In the 1964 Niigata earthquake, apartment buildings tipped over because of liquefaction.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><rect x='6' y='6' width='150' height='188' rx='6' fill='var(--c3)' fill-opacity='0.14' stroke='var(--c3)' stroke-width='1.5'/><rect x='164' y='6' width='150' height='188' rx='6' fill='var(--c2)' fill-opacity='0.14' stroke='var(--c2)' stroke-width='1.5'/><text x='81' y='28' font-size='13' fill='var(--c3)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>Solid rock</text><text x='239' y='28' font-size='13' fill='var(--c2)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>Loose, wet ground</text><path d='M20 120 Q35 112 50 120 T80 120 T110 120 T140 120' fill='none' stroke='var(--c3)' stroke-width='2'/><path d='M178 120 Q193 92 208 120 T238 120 T268 120 T298 120' fill='none' stroke='var(--c2)' stroke-width='2'/><text x='81' y='150' font-size='11' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>short period,</text><text x='81' y='166' font-size='11' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>small shaking</text><text x='239' y='150' font-size='11' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>wave slows and grows;</text><text x='239' y='166' font-size='11' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>long period: tall</text><text x='239' y='182' font-size='11' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>buildings at risk</text><text x='81' y='60' font-size='10.5' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>no amplification</text><text x='239' y='60' font-size='10.5' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>amplification</text></svg>
cards.key: Long periods put stress on tall buildings. In the same earthquake, damage in two neighboring districts can be very different because of the ground.

cards.p: A resistant building needs solid ground, good concrete and proper reinforcement. A seismic isolator separates the building from the ground and lengthens its period. In skyscrapers, a tuned mass damper damps the swaying.

cards.key: The terminal of Istanbul's Sabiha Gökçen Airport stands on isolators. The goal is not a building that never sways. It is a building that stays standing without loss of life.

cards.p: During the shaking, drop, cover and hold on. That means get down, protect your head and neck, and hold on to something sturdy. Stay away from windows, shelves and elevators. Do not run for the stairs.

cards.key: Fasten cabinets to the wall ahead of time, prepare an emergency kit, and agree on a meeting place. Preparation is the only real protection.

once.soru: You are at home and the shaking starts. What do you do first?

secenekler.neden: You get down, protect your head and hold on to something sturdy. That protects you from falling objects.
You can fall on the stairs during the shaking. Stairs are among the places that take the most damage.
The glass can break. So stay away from windows.

cards.p:
• An earthquake is the sudden release of stress on a fault.
• First P, then S, then the surface waves arrive.
• S waves do not pass through liquids.
• The distance is about 8 km × Δt.
• When the magnitude goes up by 1, the energy goes up about 32 times.
• When the periods are close, there is resonance.

quiz.q: Put the waves in the order they arrive at a station (first to arrive on top).
quiz.e: The P wave is the fastest (about 6 km/s). The S wave follows it (about 3.5 km/s). Surface waves are the slowest, but their amplitudes are the largest.

quiz.q: At a station, 12 s pass between P and S. About how many km away is the earthquake? (Each second ≈ 8 km)
quiz.e: The distance is about 8 km × 12 = 96 km. Finding the exact location of the earthquake takes at least three stations.

quiz.q: Match the terms with their definitions.
ciftler: The deep point where the break starts
The surface directly above the focus
A measure of the energy released
Shaking and damage at one place
quiz.e: Every earthquake has a single magnitude. Intensity changes from place to place. It is high near the epicenter and on loose ground.

quiz.q: In an earthquake, the period of the ground shaking is about 1 s. Which building on the same street is closest to resonance?
quiz.e: The natural period is about 0.1 × the number of floors. So the period of the 10-story building is about 1 s. The period of the shaking equals it, so this building sways the most.
y: The period of a 3-story building is about 0.3 s. That is far from the 1 s shaking.
The period of a 20-story building is about 2 s. That is twice the period of the shaking.
Every building has a different natural period. So buildings respond differently to the shaking.
